# SnapDisk — Photo Backup to USB

SnapDisk is a free Android app that backs up photos and videos to a USB disk. Plug in a USB disk, tap Backup in the notification, and photos copy oldest-first in the background — no account, no cloud, no ads. Free core (manual backup, 5 GB per run); SnapDisk Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase for auto-backup on disk connect and unlimited backup size.

## How it works

1. Plug in a USB disk. SnapDisk offers a backup in a notification: "External storage is connected. Backup photos?"
2. Tap Backup. Photos and videos copy oldest-first, in the background, with a live progress notification — percent, size, speed, time left — and Pause / Stop.
3. Trust the counts. Every file is size-verified after copying. Unplug mid-copy and it pauses, then resumes where it stopped. Already-copied files are never copied twice.

## What you get

- One tap: disk connected, notification, Backup. No account, no cloud, no upload — everything stays on your devices.
- Oldest first: your earliest photos copy first, and the folder structure is kept (Camera, Screenshots, …).
- Honest progress: the notification shows real percent, copied / total size, speed and time left. Pause and resume any time.
- Proves it copied: every file is size-verified after copying. A bad file is retried once, then skipped with its reason — it never stalls the whole backup.
- Full errors, not one line: a file too big for FAT32 is skipped and listed, not a dead end. Errors show the full error with Copy.
- Simple settings: open the app and you get a settings screen only — a From folder and a To folder, each with a folder picker.

## Pricing

- Free ($0): manual backup of photos and videos, oldest first, background copy, 5 GB per backup run. No ads, no account, no cloud.
- SnapDisk Pro ($9.99, one-time): auto-backup when a disk is connected, unlimited backup size, everything in Free. No subscription.

## Privacy

SnapDisk has no account, no ads, and no tracking. Copying runs entirely on your phone — the app does not even have internet permission, so your photos cannot leave your device. Full text: https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/privacy.html

## Questions

- Is SnapDisk really free? Yes. The free version backs up photos and videos manually, up to 5 GB per backup run, with no ads, no account, and no cloud. SnapDisk Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase that adds auto-backup when a disk is connected and unlimited backup size. There is no subscription.
- Does SnapDisk upload my photos anywhere? No. Copying runs entirely on your device, from your internal storage to the external disk you choose. The app has no internet permission, so your photos cannot leave your device.
- How does a backup start? Plug in a USB disk and SnapDisk offers a backup in a notification. Tap Backup and walk away — photos and videos copy oldest-first, in the background, with a live progress notification.
- What happens if I unplug the disk mid-copy? The backup pauses with the full error shown and resumes where it stopped when the disk is back. Files that already copied are never copied twice.
- Is SnapDisk on Google Play yet? Not yet — the Play listing is being prepared. Until then, install the APK from this page. It needs Android 7.0 or later.
- Something does not work. Where do I report it? Open an issue on GitHub — every report gets an answer: https://github.com/dzianisv/photo-backup/issues

## Guides

### How to back up photos to a USB drive without uploading them

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/backup-photos-to-usb.html

Your photos don't need a cloud to be safe. A USB drive plugged into your phone holds the whole backup — no upload, no monthly fee, no account, and nobody else's server ever sees your pictures.

TL;DR: Plug a USB drive into your Android phone and copy your photos to it. The easy way is SnapDisk: plug in the disk, tap Backup in the notification, and your photos and videos copy oldest-first in the background, with live progress and Pause / Stop. The free version covers 5 GB per run; Pro is a one-time $9.99 for auto-backup on connect and unlimited size. If you'd rather do it by hand, the Files app does the same job — just slower and with no resume if you unplug mid-copy.

What you need: an Android phone (Android 7.0 or later for SnapDisk); a USB drive your phone can read — a USB-C flash drive, or a regular USB drive with a USB-C OTG adapter (most modern Android phones support OTG; if the phone doesn't see the drive, try a different adapter); enough space on the drive for the photos you want to keep. One format note: drives formatted FAT32 can't hold a single file over 4 GB. That only matters for very long videos — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup. A drive formatted exFAT has no such limit.

Method 1: SnapDisk (one tap, background copy). SnapDisk is a free Android app that does exactly this job and nothing else. Install it from the v0.1.2 APK (it's not on Google Play yet), then: 1. Plug in the USB drive. SnapDisk offers a backup in a notification: "External storage is connected. Backup photos?" 2. Tap Backup. Photos and videos copy oldest-first — your earliest photos first — in the background, while you use the phone normally. 3. Watch the progress notification — real percent, copied / total size, speed, and time left — with Pause and Stop. You can pause and resume any time. 4. Wait for "Backup complete." Every file is size-verified after copying, so the counts are proof, not a promise. Files that already copied are never copied twice. If you unplug the drive mid-copy, the backup pauses with the full error shown and resumes where it stopped when the drive is back. If a file is corrupt or too big for FAT32, it's retried once, then skipped with its reason listed — it never stalls the whole backup. The free version backs up manually, up to 5 GB per backup run, with no ads, no account, and no cloud. SnapDisk Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase (no subscription) that starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk and removes the size limit. The app has no internet permission, so your photos physically cannot leave your device.

Method 2: by hand in the Files app (no app needed). If you'd rather not install anything, Android's built-in Files app can do the same copy: 1. Plug in the USB drive. A notification or a "USB drive" entry should appear in the Files app under Storage devices. 2. Open Files, browse to Internal storage → DCIM → Camera. That's where your phone's photos live. (Screenshots are in DCIM → Screenshots; other apps keep their own folders.) 3. Select the photos, tap ⋮ → Copy to (or Move to, if you want them off the phone), then choose the USB drive as the destination. 4. Wait for the copy to finish — and don't unplug the drive until the Files app says it's done. This works fine for a one-off copy of a few dozen photos. Its limits are the reason SnapDisk exists: no progress detail beyond a spinner, no resume if you unplug mid-copy, no verification that every file actually arrived, and you have to repeat the whole manual selection next time. For a full camera roll, the app's oldest-first background copy is the calmer option.

What to avoid: Cloud-only "backup" that uploads everything first. If the app needs an account and an upload before your photos are safe, that's not a USB backup — it's a cloud subscription with a USB step. Your photos sit on someone else's server, and the backup stops working the day you stop paying. Copying without verifying. A copy that reports "done" without checking sizes can silently leave you with half a file. Whatever method you use, spot-check a few photos on the drive before deleting them from the phone. Deleting from the phone first. A backup is only a backup once you've confirmed the copy. Copy, verify, then free the space — never the other way round.

Rule of thumb: a backup you can hold in your hand beats a backup you have to log into. Copy to the drive, check a few files open, and only then delete anything from the phone.

### USB photo backup on Android: back up photos to an external drive without uploading them

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/usb-photo-backup.html

Your phone's camera roll fits on a drive you can hold. A USB photo backup keeps the whole copy in your pocket — no upload, no monthly fee, no account, and nobody else's server ever sees your pictures.

TL;DR: To back up photos to an external drive from Android, plug a USB drive into your phone and copy them to it. ### How to back up DCIM to OTG storage on Android

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/backup-dcim-to-otg.html

DCIM is where your Android phone keeps its camera photos — and OTG is how a USB drive plugs straight into that phone. Put the two together and your whole camera roll copies to a drive you can hold, with no computer and no upload in between.

TL;DR: To back up DCIM to OTG storage on Android, plug a USB drive into your phone through an OTG adapter and copy the DCIM folder to it. The easy way is SnapDisk: plug in the drive, tap Backup in the notification, and your photos and videos copy oldest-first in the background, with live progress and Pause / Stop. The free version covers 5 GB per run; Pro is a one-time $9.99 for auto-backup on connect and unlimited size. If you'd rather do it by hand, the Files app does the same copy — just slower and with no resume if you unplug mid-copy.

What DCIM and OTG mean: DCIM is the folder Android uses for camera photos and videos, at /sdcard/DCIM. Camera shots live in DCIM → Camera; screenshots in DCIM → Screenshots. If you back up DCIM, you back up the camera roll. OTG (USB On-The-Go) lets your phone act as the host for a USB drive. Plug the drive in — directly if it's USB-C, or through a USB-C OTG adapter for a regular USB stick — and the phone reads it like a computer would. Most modern Android phones support OTG; if the phone doesn't see the drive, try a different adapter. One format note: drives formatted FAT32 can't hold a single file over 4 GB. That only matters for very long videos — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup. A drive formatted exFAT has no such limit.

What you need: an Android phone (Android 7.0 or later for SnapDisk); an OTG drive your phone can read — a USB-C flash drive, or a regular USB drive with a USB-C OTG adapter (a spinning hard drive may need its own power); enough space on the drive for the DCIM folder you want to keep. Check the drive's free space first — a phone's camera roll is often tens of gigabytes.

Method 1: SnapDisk (one tap, background copy). SnapDisk is a free Android app that does exactly this job and nothing else. Install it from the v0.1.2 APK (it's not on Google Play yet), then: 1. Plug in the OTG drive. SnapDisk offers a backup in a notification: "External storage is connected. Backup photos?" 2. Tap Backup. Photos and videos copy oldest-first — your earliest photos first — in the background, while you use the phone normally. By default it copies from /sdcard/DCIM to /disk/DCIM on the drive; both folders can be changed in Settings. 3. Watch the progress notification — real percent, copied / total size, speed, and time left — with Pause and Stop. You can pause and resume any time. 4. Wait for "Backup complete." Every file is size-verified after copying, so the counts are proof, not a promise. Files that already copied are never copied twice. If you unplug the drive mid-copy, the backup pauses with the full error shown and resumes where it stopped when the drive is back. If a file is corrupt or too big for FAT32, it's retried once, then skipped with its reason listed — it never stalls the whole backup. The free version backs up manually, up to 5 GB per backup run, with no ads, no account, and no cloud. SnapDisk Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase (no subscription) that starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk and removes the size limit. The app has no internet permission, so your photos physically cannot leave your device.

Method 2: by hand in the Files app (no app needed). If you'd rather not install anything, Android's built-in Files app can copy DCIM to the OTG drive: 1. Plug in the OTG drive. A notification or a "USB drive" entry should appear in the Files app under Storage devices. 2. Open Files, browse to Internal storage → DCIM. Long-press the DCIM folder to select the whole thing — or open DCIM → Camera and select the photos inside it. 3. Tap ⋮ → Copy to (or Move to, if you want them off the phone), then choose the external drive as the destination. 4. Wait for the copy to finish — and don't unplug the drive until the Files app says it's done. This works fine for a one-off copy. Its limits are the reason SnapDisk exists: no progress detail beyond a spinner, no resume if you unplug mid-copy, no verification that every file actually arrived, and you have to repeat the whole manual selection next time. For a full DCIM folder, the app's oldest-first background copy is the calmer option.

What to avoid: Moving instead of copying the first time. "Move to" deletes the originals as it goes. Copy first, check the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round. Copying without verifying. A copy that reports "done" without checking sizes can silently leave you with half a file. Whatever method you use, spot-check a few photos on the drive before deleting them from the phone. Unplugging mid-copy. Pulling an OTG drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight. Wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first — SnapDisk's Stop button exists for exactly this.

Rule of thumb: DCIM is the whole camera roll in one folder. Back it up as a folder, check a few files open on the drive, and only then free the space on the phone.

### How to copy photos to a USB stick on Android

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/copy-photos-to-usb-stick.html

A USB stick is the simplest photo backup there is: no account, no upload, no monthly fee — just your photos on a drive you can hold. And on Android you don't need a computer in between: the stick plugs straight into the phone.

### How to back up photos offline on Android — no cloud, no account

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/backup-photos-offline.html

Most "backup" apps start by uploading your photos to someone else's server. An offline backup never does: your photos copy from your phone straight to a drive you can hold, with no account, no upload, and nothing to log into.

TL;DR: To back up photos offline on Android, plug a USB drive into your phone and copy your photos to it — no cloud, no account, no upload. The easy way is SnapDisk: plug in the drive, tap Backup in the notification, and your photos and videos copy oldest-first in the background, with live progress and Pause / Stop. The free version covers 5 GB per run; Pro is a one-time $9.99 for auto-backup on connect and unlimited size. If you'd rather do it by hand, the Files app does the same copy — just slower and with no resume if you unplug mid-copy.

What offline backup means: An offline backup is a copy that never leaves your devices. The photos travel one hop — from your phone's storage to a USB drive in your hand — and no server, account, or internet connection is involved at any point. That is the whole difference from a cloud backup, where the first step is always an upload to someone else's computer. No upload. The copy happens over the USB cable, not the internet. It works on a plane, in a dead zone, or with mobile data off — and it costs no data. No account. Nothing to sign into, no password to lose, no terms to accept. The backup works the day you install the app and keeps working if the company behind it disappears. No tracking. With no server in the loop, there is nothing to log which photos you backed up or when. SnapDisk has no internet permission at all, so your photos physically cannot leave your device. No subscription. A drive you own is a one-time cost. A cloud backup stops working the month you stop paying — an offline backup does not. The trade-off is honest: a drive in a drawer does not protect against a house fire the way an off-site copy does. For most people the right answer is both — but the offline copy is the one that is private by construction, and it is the one this page is about.

What you need: an Android phone (Android 7.0 or later for SnapDisk); a USB drive your phone can read — a USB-C flash drive, or a regular USB drive with a USB-C OTG adapter (most modern Android phones support OTG; if the phone doesn't see the drive, try a different adapter — and note that a spinning hard drive may need its own power); enough space on the drive for the photos you want to keep. One format note: drives formatted FAT32 can't hold a single file over 4 GB. That only matters for very long videos — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup. A drive formatted exFAT has no such limit.

Method 1: SnapDisk (one tap, background copy). SnapDisk is a free Android app that does exactly this job and nothing else — and it does it entirely offline. Install it from the v0.1.2 APK (it's not on Google Play yet), then: 1. Plug in the USB drive. SnapDisk offers a backup in a notification: "External storage is connected. Backup photos?" 2. Tap Backup. Photos and videos copy oldest-first — your earliest photos first — in the background, while you use the phone normally. By default it copies from /sdcard/DCIM to /disk/DCIM on the drive; both folders can be changed in Settings. 3. Watch the progress notification — real percent, copied / total size, speed, and time left — with Pause and Stop. You can pause and resume any time. 4. Wait for "Backup complete." Every file is size-verified after copying, so the counts are proof, not a promise. Files that already copied are never copied twice. If you unplug the drive mid-copy, the backup pauses with the full error shown and resumes where it stopped when the drive is back. If a file is corrupt or too big for FAT32, it's retried once, then skipped with its reason listed — it never stalls the whole backup. The free version backs up manually, up to 5 GB per backup run, with no ads, no account, and no cloud. SnapDisk Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase (no subscription) that starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk and removes the size limit. The app has no internet permission, so your photos physically cannot leave your device.

Method 2: by hand in the Files app (no app needed). If you'd rather not install anything, Android's built-in Files app can copy your photos to the USB drive — also fully offline: 1. Plug in the USB drive. A notification or a "USB drive" entry should appear in the Files app under Storage devices. 2. Open Files, browse to Internal storage → DCIM → Camera. That's where your phone's photos live. (Screenshots are in DCIM → Screenshots; other apps keep their own folders.) 3. Select the photos, tap ⋮ → Copy to (or Move to, if you want them off the phone), then choose the USB drive as the destination. 4. Wait for the copy to finish — and don't unplug the drive until the Files app says it's done. This works fine for a one-off copy of a few dozen photos. Its limits are the reason SnapDisk exists: no progress detail beyond a spinner, no resume if you unplug mid-copy, no verification that every file actually arrived, and you have to repeat the whole manual selection next time. For a full camera roll, the app's oldest-first background copy is the calmer option. If you want the whole DCIM folder in one go, see "How to back up DCIM to OTG storage on Android".

What to avoid: Moving before verifying. "Move to" deletes the originals as it goes. Copy first, check the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round. Unplugging mid-copy. Pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight. Wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first — SnapDisk's Stop button exists for exactly this. An app that calls itself offline but asks for an account. If a backup app needs you to sign in before it copies anything, your photos are going through its servers — that is a cloud backup with an offline label. A genuinely offline app has nothing to log into and no internet permission to upload with.

Rule of thumb: if the backup works with the phone in airplane mode, it is offline. Try it — SnapDisk copies with no connection at all, because there is nothing to connect to.

### How to back up photos to an external drive on Android

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/backup-photos-to-external-drive.html

An external drive is the simplest photo backup there is: a drive you can hold, with your photos on it, and no cloud in between. On Android the drive plugs straight into the phone — no computer needed.

TL;DR: To back up photos to an external drive on Android, plug the drive into your phone and copy your photos to it — no cloud, no account, no upload. The easy way is SnapDisk: plug in the drive, tap Backup in the notification, and your photos and videos copy oldest-first in the background, with live progress and Pause / Stop. The free version covers 5 GB per run; Pro is a one-time $9.99 for auto-backup on connect and unlimited size. If you'd rather do it by hand, the Files app does the same copy — just slower and with no resume if you unplug mid-copy.

What "external drive" means on Android: An external drive is any storage that isn't built into your phone: a USB-C flash drive, a portable hard drive, or a portable SSD. Android sees it through OTG (On-The-Go) — the phone's USB-C port switches to host mode and the drive shows up as external storage, just like a memory card. Most modern Android phones support OTG; if yours doesn't see the drive, a different adapter is usually the fix. USB-C flash drive. The smallest option — plugs straight into the phone, no cable, no adapter. Good for a camera roll of a few dozen gigabytes. Portable hard drive or SSD. The roomier option — a terabyte or more for a whole photo library. Needs a USB-C OTG adapter (or a USB-C cable, for drives that have one). A spinning hard drive may need its own power; an SSD usually doesn't. One format note. Drives formatted FAT32 can't hold a single file over 4 GB. That only matters for very long videos — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup. A drive formatted exFAT has no such limit. Whichever drive you pick, the backup itself is the same: a copy from your phone's storage to the drive, with nothing uploaded anywhere. That is the whole point of an external-drive backup — the copy is yours, on hardware you hold.

What you need: an Android phone (Android 7.0 or later for SnapDisk); an external drive your phone can read — a USB-C flash drive, or a portable drive with a USB-C OTG adapter (if the phone doesn't see the drive, try a different adapter); enough space on the drive for the photos you want to keep.

Method 1: SnapDisk (one tap, background copy). SnapDisk is a free Android app that does exactly this job and nothing else — and it does it entirely offline. Install it from the v0.1.2 APK (it's not on Google Play yet), then: 1. Plug in the external drive. SnapDisk offers a backup in a notification: "External storage is connected. Backup photos?" 2. Tap Backup. Photos and videos copy oldest-first — your earliest photos first — in the background, while you use the phone normally. By default it copies from /sdcard/DCIM to /disk/DCIM on the drive; both folders can be changed in Settings. 3. Watch the progress notification — real percent, copied / total size, speed, and time left — with Pause and Stop. You can pause and resume any time. 4. Wait for "Backup complete." Every file is size-verified after copying, so the counts are proof, not a promise. Files that already copied are never copied twice. If you unplug the drive mid-copy, the backup pauses with the full error shown and resumes where it stopped when the drive is back. If a file is corrupt or too big for FAT32, it's retried once, then skipped with its reason listed — it never stalls the whole backup. The free version backs up manually, up to 5 GB per backup run, with no ads, no account, and no cloud. SnapDisk Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase (no subscription) that starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk and removes the size limit. The app has no internet permission, so your photos physically cannot leave your device.

Method 2: by hand in the Files app (no app needed). If you'd rather not install anything, Android's built-in Files app can copy your photos to the external drive — also fully offline: 1. Plug in the external drive. A notification or a "USB drive" entry should appear in the Files app under Storage devices. 2. Open Files, browse to Internal storage → DCIM → Camera. That's where your phone's photos live. (Screenshots are in DCIM → Screenshots; other apps keep their own folders.) 3. Select the photos, tap ⋮ → Copy to (or Move to, if you want them off the phone), then choose the external drive as the destination. 4. Wait for the copy to finish — and don't unplug the drive until the Files app says it's done. This works fine for a one-off copy of a few dozen photos. Its limits are the reason SnapDisk exists: no progress detail beyond a spinner, no resume if you unplug mid-copy, no verification that every file actually arrived, and you have to repeat the whole manual selection next time. For a full camera roll, the app's oldest-first background copy is the calmer option. If you want the whole DCIM folder in one go, see "How to back up DCIM to OTG storage on Android".

What to avoid: Moving before verifying. "Move to" deletes the originals as it goes. Copy first, check the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round. Unplugging mid-copy. Pulling an external drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight. Wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first — SnapDisk's Stop button exists for exactly this. An app that calls itself offline but asks for an account. If a backup app needs you to sign in before it copies anything, your photos are going through its servers — that is a cloud backup with an offline label. A genuinely offline app has nothing to log into and no internet permission to upload with.

Rule of thumb: if the backup works with the phone in airplane mode, it is offline. Try it — SnapDisk copies with no connection at all, because there is nothing to connect to.

### How to free up space by moving photos to a USB drive

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/free-up-space-move-photos-to-usb.html

Your phone is full because your photos are. Move them to a USB drive you can hold, check the copy, then delete the originals — and the storage warning goes away without losing a single picture.

TL;DR: To free up space on Android by moving photos to a USB drive, copy the photos to the drive, open a few on the drive to check they arrived, then delete the originals from the phone. The easy way to do the copy is SnapDisk: plug in the drive, tap Backup in the notification, and your photos and videos copy oldest-first in the background, with live progress and Pause / Stop. The free version covers 5 GB per run; Pro is a one-time $9.99 for auto-backup on connect and unlimited size. One honest note: SnapDisk only copies — it never deletes — so the delete step is yours, after you verify the copy. If you'd rather do it by hand, the Files app's "Move to" copies and deletes in one step — just with no resume and no verification if you unplug mid-copy.

Why photos fill the phone: On most phones, photos and videos are the single biggest thing in storage — a camera roll grows every day and never shrinks on its own. The usual fix, a cloud "free up space" button, works by uploading every photo first and deleting the local copy after. That needs an account, an upload, and a subscription to keep working. Moving the photos to a USB drive is the same idea without the cloud: the photos leave the phone, but they land on hardware you hold, not on someone else's server. The order matters more than the tool. A move is two separate acts — copy, then delete — and the only safe order is copy first, check the copy, then delete.

What you need: an Android phone (Android 7.0 or later for SnapDisk); a USB drive your phone can read — a USB-C flash drive, or a regular USB drive with a USB-C OTG adapter (most modern Android phones support OTG; if the phone doesn't see the drive, try a different adapter); enough space on the drive for the photos you want to move. Check first how much your photos take — Settings → Storage shows it — and pick a drive with room to spare.

Method 1: SnapDisk (copy first, delete after). SnapDisk is a free Android app that does exactly this job and nothing else — and it does it entirely offline. Install it from the v0.1.2 APK (it's not on Google Play yet), then: 1. Plug in the USB drive. SnapDisk offers a backup in a notification: "External storage is connected. Backup photos?" 2. Tap Backup. Photos and videos copy oldest-first — your earliest photos first — in the background, while you use the phone normally. By default it copies from /sdcard/DCIM to /disk/DCIM on the drive; both folders can be changed in Settings. 3. Watch the progress notification — real percent, copied / total size, speed, and time left — with Pause and Stop. You can pause and resume any time. 4. Wait for "Backup complete." Every file is size-verified after copying, so the counts are proof, not a promise. Files that already copied are never copied twice — so if the free 5 GB per-run limit stops a big camera roll partway, just run it again and it picks up where it left off. 5. Check the copy on the drive. Open the Files app, browse to the USB drive, and open a few photos — the oldest and the newest. If they open, the copy is good. 6. Delete the originals from the phone. In the Gallery or the Files app, select the photos you just copied and delete them. Only now is the space actually free — and only now is it safe, because the copies are verified on the drive. If you unplug the drive mid-copy, the backup pauses with the full error shown and resumes where it stopped when the drive is back. If a file is corrupt or too big for FAT32, it's retried once, then skipped with its reason listed — it never stalls the whole backup. The free version backs up manually, up to 5 GB per backup run, with no ads, no account, and no cloud. SnapDisk Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase (no subscription) that starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk and removes the size limit. The app has no internet permission, so your photos physically cannot leave your device.

Method 2: by hand in the Files app (no app needed). If you'd rather not install anything, Android's built-in Files app can move your photos to the USB drive — also fully offline: 1. Plug in the USB drive. A notification or a "USB drive" entry should appear in the Files app under Storage devices. 2. Open Files, browse to Internal storage → DCIM → Camera. That's where your phone's photos live. (Screenshots are in DCIM → Screenshots; other apps keep their own folders.) 3. Select the photos, tap ⋮ → Move to, then choose the USB drive as the destination. "Move to" copies each file and deletes the original as it goes — that is what frees the space. 4. Wait for the move to finish — and don't unplug the drive until the Files app says it's done. This works fine for a one-off move of a few dozen photos, and it frees the space in a single step. Its limits are the reason SnapDisk exists: "Move to" deletes as it copies, so a mid-move interruption can leave you with neither copy verified; there is no resume if you unplug, no verification that every file actually arrived, and you have to repeat the whole manual selection next time. For a full camera roll, the app's copy-first-then-delete flow is the safer option.

What to avoid: Deleting before verifying. A backup is only a backup once you've confirmed the copy. Copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round. "Move to" on the first try. It deletes the originals as it goes. If anything interrupts it — a loose cable, a full drive — the file in flight may be gone from both places. Copy first; move only once you trust the flow. Unplugging mid-copy. Pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight. Wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first — SnapDisk's Stop button exists for exactly this. Freeing space by deleting the only copy. A photo that exists in one place is not backed up. If the drive is the only copy left, keep it somewhere safe — a drive in a drawer is one dropped drive away from losing everything.

Rule of thumb: the copy is only a backup once you've opened a photo on the drive. Copy, check, then delete — never the other way round.

### SnapDisk vs VaultDrive: USB photo backup on Android, compared

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/snapdisk-vs-vaultdrive.html

Two Android apps that copy your photos to a USB drive — no cloud, no account, no upload. Here is how they actually differ, from the facts we could verify as of November 2026.

TL;DR: SnapDisk and VaultDrive both back up Android photos to a USB drive offline, with no account and no subscription. The verified differences: SnapDisk Pro is $9.99 one-time, half of VaultDrive Pro Lifetime at $19.99 once; SnapDisk's free tier covers 5 GB per backup run, VaultDrive's covers 200 files or 2 GB per backup; SnapDisk copies oldest-first with Pause and Stop in the progress notification; and neither app deletes photos from your phone — VaultDrive's own FAQ says freeing up space is "planned for an upcoming release", while SnapDisk's free-up-space flow is copy first, check the copy, then delete the originals yourself. VaultDrive launched in October 2026 and had about 870 installs as of November 14, 2026, with no reviews yet; SnapDisk is not on Google Play yet (v0.1.2).

SnapDisk: free Android app (v0.1.2, not on Google Play yet). Plug in the disk, tap Backup in the notification, and photos copy oldest-first in the background, size-verified, with a progress notification showing percent, copied / total size, speed, and time left, plus Pause and Stop. Free: manual backup, 5 GB per run. Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase for auto-backup when a disk is connected and unlimited size. No cloud, no account, no ads, and no internet permission.

VaultDrive: USB Photo Backup (com.coticsy.vaultdrive, by Coticsy LLC) launched in October 2026 and had about 870 installs as of November 14, 2026, with no reviews yet. Plug in a USB-C flash drive, SSD, or SD card reader, choose what to back up, and tap Start. It copies at original quality, byte for byte, keeping dates and places; offers Fresh or Incremental backup (Pro copies only what's new); resumes after unplug; checks every copy and lists skipped files with reasons; and sorts folders by date or by album. It works offline with no account, needs Android 8 or later, and shows no ads. Free tier: up to 200 files or 2 GB per backup. Pro Lifetime is $19.99 once, with no subscription, ever — verified November 16, 2026 from the vendor site (coticsy.com) and the App Store in-app purchase list.

Price: both are one-time purchases, neither charges a subscription. SnapDisk Pro $9.99 once; VaultDrive Pro Lifetime $19.99 once. SnapDisk free backs up manually up to 5 GB per backup run; VaultDrive free covers up to 200 files or 2 GB per backup. SnapDisk's runs can be repeated — files already copied are never copied twice, so a second run picks up where the first stopped.

During the backup: SnapDisk copies oldest-first in the background, with Pause and Stop in the progress notification; if you unplug mid-copy it pauses and resumes where it stopped. VaultDrive also resumes after unplug, checks every copy, and lists skipped files with reasons; on Android it keeps running in the background with a progress notification. Its Pro tier adds Incremental backup; SnapDisk skips already-copied files for free, so a repeat run only copies what's new.

Freeing up space: neither app deletes photos from your phone today. SnapDisk only copies — it never deletes — so freeing space is copy to the drive, check the copy, then delete the originals yourself (see "How to free up space by moving photos to a USB drive"). VaultDrive's own FAQ says: "Not yet. Today VaultDrive only copies, so nothing is removed from your phone. Freeing up space … is planned for an upcoming release."

What to avoid: choosing on install counts (VaultDrive had about 870 installs as of November 14, 2026, with no reviews yet; SnapDisk is not on Google Play yet, so it has no install count at all); deleting before verifying — copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone, never the other way round; assuming "offline" means the same thing everywhere (SnapDisk has no internet permission at all, so your photos physically cannot leave the device); paying for a subscription you didn't want (neither app has one).

Rule of thumb: the app that wins is the one whose copy you trust enough to delete after. Compare the price, the free tier, and the copy — then check the copy on the drive before you delete anything.

### Back up WhatsApp photos to a USB drive on Android (no computer)

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/whatsapp-photos-to-usb.html

Your WhatsApp photos are files on your phone — in a folder you can point a backup app at. Plug a USB drive into the phone and copy them straight to it, no computer, no upload.

TL;DR: Plug a USB drive into your Android phone, point SnapDisk's From folder at the WhatsApp Images folder, and tap Backup — your WhatsApp photos copy oldest-first to the drive, with no computer and no upload in between. The honest limits, up front: SnapDisk copies media files only — the photos and videos in the folder you pick, recursively. It does not back up chat history (msgstore.db.crypt14), voice notes (.opus is not a copied file type), stickers outside the picked folder, or documents. For chats, use WhatsApp's own Settings > Chats > Chat backup (Google Drive) — this article is only about the photo and video files. SnapDisk copies, it never deletes — deleting from the phone afterwards is your step, only after verifying a few photos on the drive. Free version: 5 GB per run; run it again past the cap and it picks up where it stopped, because files already copied are never copied twice. As of November 16, 2026, no top search result offers phone-to-USB WhatsApp backup without a computer: the top results are PC-based tools (Wondershare MobileTrans, Windows/Mac), SD-card moves, or cloud (Google Drive, iCloud, Google Photos).

Where WhatsApp keeps your photos: WhatsApp saves every photo you receive (and send, if you keep the default) as an ordinary file in a folder on your phone. The folder's location depends on the Android version and how WhatsApp was installed. Newer Android: Internal storage > Android > media > com.whatsapp > WhatsApp > Media > WhatsApp Images. Older installs: Internal storage > WhatsApp > Media > WhatsApp Images. Videos live next door, in WhatsApp Video under the same Media folder. You do not need to memorise either path — you navigate to the folder in a picker and tap it. If a photo never downloaded (the blurred thumbnail with a download arrow), it is not on your phone yet — open the chat and download it first, or there is nothing to copy.

What you need: an Android phone (Android 7.0 or later for SnapDisk); a USB drive your phone can read — a USB-C flash drive, or a regular USB drive with a USB-C OTG adapter (most modern Android phones support OTG; if the phone doesn't see the drive, try a different adapter); enough space on the drive for the WhatsApp photos you want to keep. One format note: drives formatted FAT32 can't hold a single file over 4 GB. That only matters for very long videos — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup. A drive formatted exFAT has no such limit.

Method 1: SnapDisk (one tap, background copy). SnapDisk is a free Android app that does exactly this job and nothing else. Install it from the v0.1.2 APK (it's not on Google Play yet), then: 1. Open SnapDisk and set the From folder. The app opens to a settings screen with a From folder and a To folder, each with a folder picker. Tap the From folder picker and navigate to the WhatsApp Images folder and tap it. To get the videos too, pick the parent Media folder instead: SnapDisk walks the folder recursively, so one run copies WhatsApp Images and WhatsApp Video together. (Other file types in that folder — documents, voice notes — are simply skipped; only image and video files copy.) 2. Set the To folder to the USB drive. Plug in the USB drive, tap the To folder picker, and choose a folder on the drive. The copy mirrors the source folder structure, so your WhatsApp Images stay in a WhatsApp Images folder on the drive. 3. Plug in the USB drive. SnapDisk offers a backup in a notification: "External storage is connected. Backup photos?" 4. Tap Backup. Photos and videos copy oldest-first — your earliest WhatsApp photos first — in the background, while you use the phone normally. 5. Watch the progress notification — real percent, copied / total size, speed, and time left — with Pause and Stop. You can pause and resume any time. 6. Wait for "Backup complete." Every file is size-verified after copying, so the counts are proof, not a promise. Files that already copied are never copied twice — so if the free 5 GB per-run limit stops a big WhatsApp folder partway, just run it again and it picks up where it left off. If you unplug the drive mid-copy, the backup pauses with the full error shown and resumes where it stopped when the drive is back. If a file is corrupt or too big for FAT32, it's retried once, then skipped with its reason listed — it never stalls the whole backup. The free version backs up manually, up to 5 GB per backup run, with no ads, no account, and no cloud. SnapDisk Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase (no subscription) that starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk and removes the size limit. The app has no internet permission, so your photos physically cannot leave your device.

Method 2: by hand in the Files app (no app needed). If you'd rather not install anything, Android's built-in Files app can copy the WhatsApp folder to the USB drive: 1. Plug in the USB drive. A notification or a "USB drive" entry should appear in the Files app under Storage devices. 2. Open Files, browse to Internal storage and find the WhatsApp folder — Android > media > com.whatsapp > WhatsApp > Media > WhatsApp Images on newer Android, or WhatsApp > Media > WhatsApp Images on older installs. 3. Select the photos (or long-press the WhatsApp Images folder to select the whole thing), tap ⋮ → Copy to, then choose the USB drive as the destination. 4. Wait for the copy to finish — and don't unplug the drive until the Files app says it's done. This works fine for a one-off copy. Its limits are the reason SnapDisk exists: no progress detail beyond a spinner, no resume if you unplug mid-copy, no verification that every file actually arrived, and you have to repeat the whole manual selection next time WhatsApp photos pile up. For a WhatsApp folder that grows every day, the app's oldest-first background copy is the calmer option.

What this does not back up: Copying the WhatsApp Images folder backs up the files — the photos and videos. It does not back up chat history (your messages live in a database file, msgstore.db.crypt14, not in the Images folder, and SnapDisk only copies image and video files — back up chats with WhatsApp's own Settings > Chats > Chat backup, which backs up to Google Drive); voice notes (.opus audio files, which SnapDisk does not copy); stickers outside the picked folder (they only copy if they sit inside the folder you picked, and only if they are image files); or documents (PDFs and other files sent in WhatsApp are not image or video files, so they are skipped). If you want the whole WhatsApp — chats and media together — the Google Drive chat backup is the route, and it is the only one WhatsApp itself supports. This article's route is for the photos and videos as files on a drive you hold.

What to avoid: PC-only tools when you have no computer (the top search results for this job are Windows/Mac programs like Wondershare MobileTrans that need a computer in between); cloud backup dressed as USB backup (if the app needs an account and an upload before your photos are safe, that's a cloud subscription with a USB step); deleting before verifying (copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round; SnapDisk only copies, it never deletes, so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check); assuming the chats came along (the photo files are not the conversation — run WhatsApp's own Chat backup too); unplugging mid-copy (pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight — wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first).

Rule of thumb: the photos are files in a folder — back up the folder. The chats are a database — back them up in WhatsApp. Do both, and check the copy on the drive before you delete anything from the phone.

### Back up Samsung Galaxy photos to a USB drive (no computer)

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/samsung-galaxy-photos-to-usb.html

Galaxy phones are the most common Android phones there are, and Samsung gives you two ways to get photos onto a USB drive — but neither one is a photo backup that runs itself. Here is what Samsung offers, and the one-tap version.

TL;DR: Plug a USB drive into your Galaxy phone, tap Backup in SnapDisk, and your whole photo library copies oldest-first to the drive in the background — with real progress (percent, GB copied / total, speed, time left), Pause and Stop, and resume where it stopped if you unplug. No computer, no upload, no account. The copies are the original files: SnapDisk streams each file byte-for-byte to the drive, never recompresses or resizes, and checks the size of every file after copying. The honest contrast, up front: Samsung's own routes work — Smart Switch backs the whole device up to a USB drive, and My Files copies photos by hand — but Smart Switch is a whole-device backup, not a photo library you can re-run, and My Files has no progress detail, no resume, and no verification. And one honest correction to the brief behind this article: the original-quality angle alone is not an open gap — the rival app Photos to USB: OTG Backup already advertises byte-for-byte originals on its Play listing — so this article targets the Galaxy query instead, where no top result automates the photo library. SnapDisk copies, it never deletes — deleting from the phone afterwards is your step, only after verifying a few photos on the drive. Free version: 5 GB per run; run it again past the cap and it picks up where it stopped, because files already copied are never copied twice. As of November 16, 2026, no top search result for this query offers an automated whole-library photo backup with progress, Pause/Stop, and resume: the top results are Samsung's Smart Switch whole-device backup, My Files manual copy, PC drag-and-drop, or cloud.

What the search results actually offer: search "back up photos from Samsung Galaxy to USB flash drive without computer" and every top result teaches one of Samsung's own routes, or the same manual job. Smart Switch (umatechnology.org, summarising Samsung's support pages) — connect the drive, open Smart Switch, tap the external-storage icon, choose Back up, pick photos and videos; it works and needs no computer, but it is a whole-device backup, and Samsung's own pages note categories Smart Switch may not save on every phone. My Files (sekin.in; Samsung Members) — plug the drive in, open My Files, pick the photos, Copy, choose USB storage, Copy here: manual select-copy-paste, and Samsung says files cannot be transferred directly to the USB drive from apps such as Gallery. Coolmuster — four ways: drag-and-drop through a computer, OTG copy in the file manager, a PC tool, or cloud storage; three of the four need a computer or a cloud account. Cloud routes — Samsung Cloud and Google Photos back up over Wi-Fi, not to a drive you hold; Samsung Cloud's own guide notes files larger than 1 GB cannot be backed up to it, and Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos. None of them offers an automated photo-library backup: nothing that takes the entire camera roll, copies it oldest-first in the background, shows progress, pauses and resumes, and verifies every file.

What you need: a Samsung Galaxy phone (Android 7.0 or later for SnapDisk); a USB drive your phone can read — a USB-C flash drive plugs straight into a modern Galaxy phone, or a regular USB drive with a USB-C OTG adapter (Samsung's own Type-A-to-Type-C adapter supports OTG, and one usually comes in the box); enough space on the drive for the photos you want to keep. One format note: drives formatted FAT32 can't hold a single file over 4 GB. That only matters for very long videos — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup. A drive formatted exFAT has no such limit.

Method 1: SnapDisk (one tap, background copy). SnapDisk is a free Android app that does exactly this job and nothing else. Install it from the v0.1.2 APK (it's not on Google Play yet), then: 1. Open SnapDisk and check the folders. The app opens to a settings screen with a From folder and a To folder, each with a folder picker. The defaults are already right for most people: From /sdcard/DCIM (your camera photos — Galaxy camera photos live in DCIM/Camera), To /disk/DCIM on the drive. If your photos live somewhere else, tap the From picker and choose that folder — the picker is the Android system folder picker, and the app keeps access to it. 2. Plug in the USB drive. SnapDisk offers a backup in a notification: "External storage is connected. Backup photos?" 3. Tap Backup. Your whole library copies oldest-first — your earliest photos first — in the background, while you use the phone normally. The copy mirrors the source folder structure on the drive, so DCIM stays DCIM. 4. Watch the progress notification — real percent, copied / total size, speed, and time left — with Pause and Stop. You can pause and resume any time. 5. Wait for "Backup complete." Every file is size-verified after copying, so the counts are proof, not a promise. Files that already copied are never copied twice — so if the free 5 GB per-run limit stops a big library partway, just run it again and it picks up where it left off. The copies are the original files. SnapDisk streams each file byte-for-byte from the phone to the drive — the code reads the file and writes the same bytes out, with no decode, no recompression, and no resize — and then checks that the copy on the drive is the same size as the original. A rival app, Photos to USB: OTG Backup, does the same byte-for-byte copy and says so on its Play listing; SnapDisk is not the only app that preserves originals, and this article does not claim it is. What SnapDisk adds over that rival is the automated whole-library run: oldest-first order, progress with Pause and Stop, resume where it stopped, and skip-if-already-copied on the next run. If a file is corrupt or too big for FAT32, it's retried once, then skipped with its reason listed — it never stalls the whole backup. The free version backs up manually, up to 5 GB per backup run, with no ads, no account, and no cloud. SnapDisk Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase (no subscription) that starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk and removes the size limit. The app has no internet permission, so your photos physically cannot leave your device.

Method 2: Smart Switch (Samsung's own route, no app needed). If you'd rather use Samsung's own tool, Smart Switch backs up to a USB drive with no computer: 1. Connect the USB drive to the Galaxy phone, using an OTG adapter if needed. 2. Open Smart Switch. 3. Tap the external storage or SD card icon. 4. Select Back up (if the screen has a "Back up to" option, choose the storage you connected). 5. Choose photos and videos and let it run. This works fine for a one-off backup of the phone. Its limits are the reason SnapDisk exists for photos: Smart Switch backs up the whole device rather than running a photo-library backup you repeat, its own pages note categories it may not save on every phone, and there is no oldest-first photo order, no per-file progress detail, and no resume-and-skip on the next run — you repeat the whole backup instead of picking up where the last one stopped.

Method 3: by hand in My Files (no app needed). Samsung's file manager can copy your photos to the USB drive: 1. Plug in the USB drive. 2. Open My Files. 3. Select the photos (long-press the first, tap the rest, or long-press a folder to select the whole thing) — do it in My Files, not in Gallery, which Samsung says cannot transfer directly to USB. 4. Tap Copy, choose USB storage, tap Copy here. 5. Unmount the USB storage in My Files before disconnecting it. This works fine for a one-off copy. Its limits are the reason SnapDisk exists: you pick files one by one, there is no progress detail beyond a spinner, no resume if you unplug mid-copy, no verification that every file actually arrived, and you have to repeat the whole manual selection next time photos pile up. For a library that grows every day, the app's oldest-first background copy is the calmer option.

What this does not do: photos and videos only (SnapDisk copies image and video files; documents, voice notes, and anything that isn't a photo or video is skipped — Smart Switch is the tool if you want the whole device, not just photos); only the folder you pick (by default DCIM — your camera photos; photos in other folders only copy if you point the From folder at them, or at a parent folder that contains them); free 5 GB per run (a library bigger than 5 GB stops at the cap; run it again and it picks up where it stopped; Pro, $9.99 one-time, removes the limit and starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk); files over 4 GB on FAT32 are skipped (very long videos on a FAT32 drive are listed with their reason instead of failing the backup — reformat the drive to exFAT if you need them); it never deletes (SnapDisk only copies — freeing space on the phone is copy, check the copy on the drive, then delete the originals yourself, never the other way round); not the only byte-for-byte copier (Photos to USB: OTG Backup also copies originals without compression; SnapDisk's difference is the automated library run — oldest-first, progress, Pause/Stop, resume — not the quality claim alone).

What to avoid: PC-only tools when you have no computer (drag-and-drop through a Windows PC needs the PC in between); cloud backup dressed as USB backup (if the app needs an account and an upload before your photos are safe, that's a cloud subscription with a USB step); deleting before verifying (copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round; SnapDisk only copies, it never deletes, so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check); moving instead of copying (the file manager's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step — if the copy fails halfway, photos are already gone from the phone; copy first, verify, then delete); unplugging mid-copy (pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight — wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first).

Rule of thumb: if you have to pick the files yourself, it isn't a backup — it's a chore you will skip. Automate the copy, check it on the drive, then delete from the phone.

### Back up Google Pixel photos to a USB drive (no computer)

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/google-pixel-photos-to-usb.html

Pixel phones have no SD-card slot and no Samsung-style file manager — but a USB-C flash drive plugs straight in, and the stock route is Files by Google. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

TL;DR: Plug a USB drive into your Pixel phone, tap Backup in SnapDisk, and your whole photo library copies oldest-first to the drive in the background — with real progress (percent, GB copied / total, speed, time left), Pause and Stop, and resume where it stopped if you unplug. No computer, no upload, no account. The copies are the original files: SnapDisk streams each file byte-for-byte to the drive, never recompresses or resizes, and checks the size of every file after copying. The honest contrast, up front: Files by Google works — it is the stock file manager on a Pixel, and it copies photos to a USB drive — but it is manual select-copy-paste with no progress detail, no resume, and no verification; and Google Photos backup is a cloud copy, not a USB copy. SnapDisk copies, it never deletes — deleting from the phone afterwards is your step, only after verifying a few photos on the drive. Free version: 5 GB per run; run it again past the cap and it picks up where it stopped, because files already copied are never copied twice. What the search results actually offer: search "back up photos from Google Pixel to USB flash drive without computer" and every top result teaches the same manual job, in different packaging. YouTube (PYcbV25CczI) — plug the drive in via OTG, open the phone's built-in file manager, select photos in DCIM, Move or Copy to the drive: manual select-copy-paste, and it suggests Move, which deletes the originals as it goes. AnExplorer (anexplorer.io/transfer/phone-to-usb) — connect the drive with an OTG adapter, open AnExplorer, long-press to select files in DCIM/Camera, Copy, Paste to the drive: a thorough manual guide, and still manual, with no resume or verification. CellularNews — connect the drive with an OTG adapter, then copy or move the photos using the Files app: the Files app on a Pixel is Files by Google, and the copy is by hand. Dr.Fone (drfone.wondershare.com) — four ways: Google Drive, PC drag-and-drop, OTG copy in the file manager, or AirDroid over Wi-Fi; three of the four need a computer or a cloud account, and the OTG way is the same manual file-manager copy. Manual do Bruxo — Files by Google, step by step: plug the drive in, open Files, Browse, Images, select, Copy to, choose the USB drive: the clearest Pixel-specific guide of the five, and it still ends with you selecting photos one by one. Cloud routes — Google Photos backs up over Wi-Fi to Google's servers, not to a drive you hold; its "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, and a cloud backup stops working the day you stop paying for storage. None of them offers an automated photo-library backup: nothing that takes the entire camera roll, copies it oldest-first in the background, shows progress, pauses and resumes, and verifies every file.

Method 2: Files by Google (the stock route, no app needed). Pixel phones ship with Files by Google, and it can copy your photos to the USB drive: 1. Plug in the USB drive — a "USB drive connected" notification should appear. 2. Open Files, go to Browse, then Images — or Internal storage, DCIM, Camera, where your camera photos live. 3. Select the photos (long-press the first, tap the rest, or tap Select all). 4. Tap the three dots and choose Copy to, then select the USB drive. 5. Wait for the copy to finish, and don't unplug the drive until the Files app says it's done. Use Copy, not Move: Move deletes the originals as it goes, so a bumped cable halfway through loses photos. This works fine for a one-off copy. Method 3: through a computer (if you have one). If a PC or Mac is handy, the old route still works: plug the Pixel into the computer with a USB cable, set the phone to File Transfer mode, and drag the DCIM folder onto the USB drive — or use a tool like Dr.Fone to bulk-export the photos first. This works fine, and it is the only route above that needs a second device in between. If the phone and the drive are all you have, Method 1 or 2 is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 16, 2026.

The toggle switches itself off again if no drive is connected within 10 minutes, so enable it with the drive already attached. Second, the stock file manager on recent OnePlus phones is My Files, not Files by Google — and most OnePlus phones have no microSD slot, so a USB drive is the plug-in storage you get. What the search results actually offer: search "back up photos from Xiaomi to USB flash drive without computer" and every top result teaches the same manual job, in different packaging. AnExplorer (anexplorer.io/transfer/phone-to-usb) — connect the drive with an OTG adapter, open AnExplorer, long-press to select files in DCIM/Camera, Copy, Paste to the drive: a thorough manual guide, and the only one of the five that shows a progress bar with speed and time remaining — but it is still a manual copy, with no resume or verification. FoneLab — OTG manual copy in the Files app (select photos, Copy or Move to the flash drive), a PC tool (FoneLab HyperTrans, phone and drive both plugged into the computer), or Samsung Smart Switch: the OTG way is the same manual file-manager copy, and the other two need a computer. Dr.Fone (drfone.wondershare.com) — four ways: Google Drive, PC drag-and-drop, OTG copy in the file manager, or AirDroid over Wi-Fi; three of the four need a computer or a cloud account, and the OTG way is the same manual file-manager copy. YouTube (PYcbV25CczI) — plug the drive in via OTG, open the phone's built-in file manager, select photos in DCIM, Move or Copy to the drive: manual select-copy-paste, and it suggests Move, which deletes the originals as it goes. EpicTechTips — plug the drive in, open the file manager, select photos, Move to the drive; or use a PC as a middleman, or cloud storage: the direct way is the same manual file-manager copy, and it too suggests Move. Cloud routes — Google Photos backs up over Wi-Fi to Google's servers, not to a drive you hold; its "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, and a cloud backup stops working the day you stop paying for storage. None of them offers an automated photo-library backup: nothing that takes the entire camera roll, copies it oldest-first in the background, shows progress, pauses and resumes, and verifies every file.

What you need: a Xiaomi, Redmi, or POCO phone (Android 7.0 or later for SnapDisk); a USB drive your phone can read — a USB-C flash drive plugs straight into a modern Xiaomi phone, or a regular USB drive with a USB-C OTG adapter; enough space on the drive for the photos you want to keep. Two Xiaomi specifics: first, OTG is off by default on many MIUI and HyperOS phones — before the phone will see any drive, enable it in Settings, Additional settings, OTG (on some phones: Settings, More settings, OTG). The switch turns itself off again after about 10 minutes without a drive, so enable it with the drive already attached. One honest wrinkle: Xiaomi's own support note says the OTG switch was removed from MIUI 11 onward on some versions, while newer model-specific pages still document a toggle (for example on the Xiaomi 14T) — so if your phone has no OTG switch, don't assume it is broken: on those phones OTG works directly, no toggle needed. Second, the stock file manager on Xiaomi phones is Mi File Manager, and the stock gallery is Gallery — and the microSD slot varies by model: most Redmi and Redmi Note phones have one, while POCO F-series phones and Xiaomi flagships often don't, so check your own model's specs. If your phone has no microSD slot, a USB drive is the plug-in storage you get. One format note: drives formatted FAT32 can't hold a single file over 4 GB. That only matters for very long videos — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup. A drive formatted exFAT has no such limit.

Method 1: SnapDisk (one tap, background copy). SnapDisk is a free Android app that does exactly this job and nothing else. Install it from the v0.1.2 APK (it's not on Google Play yet), then: 1. Open SnapDisk and check the folders. The app opens to a settings screen with a From folder and a To folder, each with a folder picker. The defaults are already right for most people: From /sdcard/DCIM (your camera photos — Xiaomi camera photos live in DCIM/Camera), To /disk/DCIM on the drive. If your photos live somewhere else, tap the From picker and choose that folder — the picker is the Android system folder picker, and the app keeps access to it. 2. Enable OTG, then plug in the USB drive. If your phone has the switch, go to Settings, Additional settings, OTG and switch it on (on some phones: Settings, More settings, OTG), then plug the drive in with the toggle still on. If there is no OTG switch, just plug the drive in — OTG works directly on those phones. SnapDisk offers a backup in a notification: "External storage is connected. Backup photos?" 3. Tap Backup. Your whole library copies oldest-first — your earliest photos first — in the background, while you use the phone normally. The copy mirrors the source folder structure on the drive, so DCIM stays DCIM. 4. Watch the progress notification — real percent, copied / total size, speed, and time left — with Pause and Stop. You can pause and resume any time. 5. Wait for "Backup complete." Every file is size-verified after copying, so the counts are proof, not a promise. Files that already copied are never copied twice — so if the free 5 GB per-run limit stops a big library partway, just run it again and it picks up where it left off. The copies are the original files. SnapDisk streams each file byte-for-byte from the phone to the drive — the code reads the file and writes the same bytes out, with no decode, no recompression, and no resize — and then checks that the copy on the drive is the same size as the original. Other apps copy originals byte-for-byte too; what SnapDisk adds is the automated whole-library run: oldest-first order, progress with Pause and Stop, resume where it stopped, and skip-if-already-copied on the next run. If a file is corrupt or too big for FAT32, it's retried once, then skipped with its reason listed — it never stalls the whole backup. The free version backs up manually, up to 5 GB per backup run, with no ads, no account, and no cloud. SnapDisk Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase (no subscription) that starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk and removes the size limit. The app has no internet permission, so your photos physically cannot leave your device.

Method 2: Mi File Manager (the stock route, no app needed). Xiaomi phones ship with Mi File Manager, and it can copy your photos to the USB drive: 1. Enable OTG if your phone has the switch — Settings, Additional settings, OTG (on some phones: Settings, More settings, OTG). If the phone ignores the drive completely, this toggle is the reason. 2. Plug in the USB drive — a "USB drive connected" notification should appear. 3. Open Mi File Manager, then Photos — or Internal storage, DCIM, Camera, where your camera photos live. 4. Select the photos (long-press the first, tap the rest, or tap Select all). 5. Tap Copy, then select the USB drive, and wait for the copy to finish — don't unplug the drive until Mi File Manager says it's done. Use Copy, not Move: Move deletes the originals as it goes, so a bumped cable halfway through loses photos. This works fine for a one-off copy. Its limits are the reason SnapDisk exists: you pick files one by one, there is no progress detail beyond a spinner, no resume if you unplug mid-copy, no verification that every file actually arrived, and you have to repeat the whole manual selection next time photos pile up. For a library that grows every day, the app's oldest-first background copy is the calmer option.

Method 3: through a computer (if you have one). If a PC or Mac is handy, the old route still works: plug the Xiaomi phone into the computer with a USB cable, tap the USB notification and choose File transfer (by default a Xiaomi phone charges only) — and drag the DCIM folder onto the USB drive, or use a tool like Dr.Fone or Xiaomi's own Mi PC Suite to bulk-export the photos first. This works fine, and it is the only route above that needs a second device in between. If the phone and the drive are all you have, Method 1 or 2 is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 16, 2026.

What this does not do: photos and videos only (SnapDisk copies image and video files; documents, voice notes, and anything that isn't a photo or video is skipped); only the folder you pick (by default DCIM — your camera photos; photos in other folders only copy if you point the From folder at them, or at a parent folder that contains them); free 5 GB per run (a library bigger than 5 GB stops at the cap; run it again and it picks up where it stopped; Pro, $9.99 one-time, removes the limit and starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk); files over 4 GB on FAT32 are skipped (very long videos on a FAT32 drive are listed with their reason instead of failing the backup — reformat the drive to exFAT if you need them); it never deletes (SnapDisk only copies — freeing space on the phone is copy, check the copy on the drive, then delete the originals yourself, never the other way round).

What to avoid: enabling OTG and then waiting (on phones that have the OTG switch, it turns itself off again after about 10 minutes without a drive — enable it with the drive already attached, or re-enable it and plug the drive in straight away; if the phone ignores a drive you just plugged in, check the toggle first; if your phone has no OTG switch, that is normal on some MIUI versions — OTG works directly there, so look elsewhere for the problem); PC-only tools when you have no computer (drag-and-drop through a Windows PC needs the PC in between); cloud backup dressed as USB backup (if the app needs an account and an upload before your photos are safe, that's a cloud subscription with a USB step); deleting before verifying (copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round; SnapDisk only copies, it never deletes, so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check); moving instead of copying (the file manager's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step — if the copy fails halfway, photos are already gone from the phone; copy first, verify, then delete); unplugging mid-copy (pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight — wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first).

Rule of thumb: if you have to pick the files yourself, it isn't a backup — it's a chore you will skip. Automate the copy, check it on the drive, then delete from the phone.

### Back up Motorola photos to a USB drive (no computer)

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/motorola-photos-to-usb.html

Motorola phones run near-stock Android, so there is no OTG switch to hunt for — a USB-C flash drive plugs straight in, and the stock route is Files by Google. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

TL;DR: On a Moto G or Motorola Edge phone, plug a USB drive in, tap Backup in SnapDisk, and your whole photo library copies oldest-first to the drive in the background — with real progress (percent, GB copied / total, speed, time left), Pause and Stop, and resume where it stopped if you unplug. No computer, no upload, no account. The copies are the original files: SnapDisk streams each file byte-for-byte to the drive, never recompresses or resizes, and checks the size of every file after copying. The honest contrast, up front: Files by Google works — it is the stock file manager on recent Motorola phones, and it copies photos to a USB drive — but it is manual select-copy-paste with no progress detail, no resume, and no verification; and Google Photos backup is a cloud copy, not a USB copy. SnapDisk copies, it never deletes — deleting from the phone afterwards is your step, only after verifying a few photos on the drive. Free version: 5 GB per run; run it again past the cap and it picks up where it stopped, because files already copied are never copied twice. As of November 16, 2026, no top search result for this query offers an automated whole-library photo backup with progress, Pause/Stop, and resume: the top results are a YouTube OTG walkthrough, an AnExplorer manual guide, Dr.Fone's PC and cloud routes, a MobiKin PC tool and manual copy, or a thegadgetians manual guide.

What the search results actually offer: search "back up photos from Motorola to USB flash drive without computer" and every top result teaches the same manual job, in different packaging. YouTube (PYcbV25CczI) — plug the drive in via OTG, open the phone's built-in file manager, select photos in DCIM, Move or Copy to the drive: manual select-copy-paste, and it suggests Move, which deletes the originals as it goes; its own guide names the file manager on a Motorola as Files, or Files by Google. AnExplorer (anexplorer.io/transfer/phone-to-usb) — connect the drive with an OTG adapter, open AnExplorer, long-press to select files in DCIM/Camera, Copy, Paste to the drive: a thorough manual guide, and the only one of the five that shows a progress bar with speed and time remaining — but it is still a manual copy, with no resume or verification. Dr.Fone (drfone.wondershare.com) — four ways: Google Drive, PC drag-and-drop, OTG copy in the file manager, or AirDroid over Wi-Fi; three of the four need a computer or a cloud account, and the OTG way is the same manual file-manager copy. MobiKin — PC drag-and-drop, a PC tool (MobiKin Assistant for Android), OTG manual copy, Files by Google, or AirDroid: the PC ways need a computer, and the phone-only ways are the same manual select-copy-paste. YouTube (ch1evyu5PPM) — plug the drive in via OTG, open the file manager, select photos in DCIM, Copy or Move to the drive: manual select-copy-paste again, and it too suggests Move. TheGadgetians — connect the drive with an OTG adapter, open the file manager, select and copy files, paste onto the drive: the same manual copy, plus a mention of ThePhotoStick Omni, a dedicated stick with its own app, not an ordinary flash drive. None of them offers an automated photo-library backup: nothing that takes the entire camera roll, copies it oldest-first in the background, shows progress, pauses and resumes, and verifies every file.

What you need: a Moto G or Motorola Edge phone (Android 7.0 or later for SnapDisk); a USB drive your phone can read — a USB-C flash drive plugs straight into a modern Motorola phone, or a regular USB drive with a USB-C OTG adapter; enough space on the drive for the photos you want to keep. Two Motorola specifics: first, there is no OTG switch to enable. Motorola runs near-stock Android, so unlike OnePlus or Xiaomi there is no "OTG connection" toggle hiding in Settings — plug the drive in and the phone mounts it on its own, with a "USB available" notification and the drive listed under Storage devices in Files by Google. If the phone shows no reaction at all, check the USB notification: if it says the phone is charging a connected device, tap it and switch "Controlled by" to "This device". Second, the stock file manager on recent Motorola phones is Files by Google, and the stock gallery is Google Photos — and the microSD slot varies by model: most Moto G phones have one (up to 1 TB on recent models), while the Motorola Edge 2024 and 2025 have no expandable storage at all, so check your own model's specs. If your phone has no microSD slot, a USB drive is the plug-in storage you get. One format note: drives formatted FAT32 can't hold a single file over 4 GB. That only matters for very long videos — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup. A drive formatted exFAT has no such limit.

Plug in the USB drive — a "USB available" notification should appear; tap it, then tap the drive and Allow. 2. Open Files by Google, scroll to Storage devices, and tap your USB drive to confirm it mounted. 3. Go back to Internal storage, DCIM, Camera, where your camera photos live. 4. Select the photos (long-press the first, tap the rest, or tap the three dots and Select all). 5.
