FoneLab (fonelab.com/resource/how-to-transfer-photos-from-android-phone-to-usb-flash-drive.html) — OTG adapter copy, a PC file-explorer copy, or the FoneLab HyperTrans PC tool; generic Android, and two of the three ways need a computer. MobileTrans (mobiletrans.wondershare.com/android-tips/how-to-transfer-files-via-otg.html) — connect the phone and the pen drive with an OTG cable, select the files, Copy, Paste to the drive; generic Android, not written for Asus. TechDows (techdows.com/usb-otg-everything-you-need-to-know.html) — a general OTG explainer: which adapter to buy, how to open OTG storage, and what to do when a drive does not show up; useful background, not an Asus guide. mobilespecs.net (mobilespecs.net/phone/backup/ASUS/ASUS_ZenFone_4_ZE554KL.html) — the one Asus-specific backup page found in the wider search, and it is not a phone-to-USB guide at all: sync data to Google's cloud, back photos up with Google Photos, or use TWRP Recovery, Titanium Backup, or ADB — a PC, a custom recovery, or the cloud, never a USB drive. devicesfaq (devicesfaq.com — Asus Zenfone 9 and Zenfone 7 FAQ pages) — the Asus-specific backup answers found in the wider search: copy files to a computer over USB, back up to Google Drive's cloud, or use Google Photos for photos and videos; a PC or a cloud, never a USB drive. manualsnet (manualsnet.com/asus/zenfone-selfie-zd551kl) — the Asus-specific transfer answer found in the wider search: connect the phone to a computer with a USB cable, choose File Transfer mode, and copy the photos on the computer; a PC in between, not a phone-to-USB copy. ASUS Phone Clone (Play listing, com.futuredial.asusdatatransfer) — Asus's own migration app (formerly ASUS Data Transfer): it moves contacts, messages, photos, videos, music, files, and apps from an old Android phone to a new Asus phone over Wi-Fi, with no cable and no mobile network; phone-to-phone, not phone-to-USB — and Asus's own FAQ says stock-AOSP Zenfones (Max Pro, Max Pro M2, Live L1, Live L2) are not supported at all. Asus's own FAQ (asus.com/in/support/faq/1043100/) — confirms Phone Clone (Data Transfer) is a migration tool for a new Asus phone, covering Zenfone 6 through Zenfone 10 and ROG Phone 3 through ROG Phone 7; it moves data to a phone, not to a USB drive. ZenTalk (zentalk.asus.com) — Asus's own forum: on Zenfone 9 and 10 the default gallery is Asus's own Gallery app, and Google Photos cannot be set as the default; the stock gallery on recent Zenfones is Asus Gallery, not Google Photos. Zenfone 5 Selfie manual (gebruikershandleiding.com) — Asus's own manual for the stock file manager: File Manager "allows you to easily locate and manage your data on the internal storage of your ASUS Phone and its connected external storage devices", launched from ASUS > File Manager; the stock file manager on Asus phones handles USB drives — it just copies by hand. Notebookcheck's Zenfone 7 Pro review — the one Asus-specific OTG confirmation from a review: the Zenfone 7 Pro's USB-C port "supports USB OTG, which enables users to connect to peripherals and external storage devices", ZenUI 7 is "only minimally different to standard Android", and the phone ships with "an audio recorder, a file manager and the tool Asus Data Transfer" preinstalled. OTG spec sheets — the wider search confirms OTG on most Zenfones but not all of them: the Zenfone 3 Laser is listed as "OTG Compatible, Yes" (Flipkart), the Zenfone 6 lists OTG in its specifications, and the Zenfone 4 and Zenfone 3 Max reviews confirm OTG — but the original Zenfone 5 "doesn't support USB OTG" (91mobiles) and the Zenfone 2 lists "USB OTG — No"; check your own model's specs before buying an adapter. Google Photos (Play listing, com.google.android.apps.photos) — Google's own photo backup: 15 GB of cloud storage free with every Google account, automatic upload over Wi-Fi; cloud, not a USB copy. Cloud routes — Google Photos backs up over Wi-Fi to Google's servers, not to a drive you hold; its "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, and a cloud backup stops working the day you stop paying for storage. Asus's own cloud is WebStorage — 5 GB free with older Zenfones — and it has the same limit: it backs the phone up to Asus's servers, not to a USB drive. None of them is an Asus-specific guide at all, and none of them offers an automated Asus photo-library backup: nothing that takes the entire camera roll, copies it oldest-first in the background as plain files you can open anywhere, shows progress, pauses and resumes, and verifies every file.

What you need: an Asus phone (Android 7.0 or later for SnapDisk); a USB drive your phone can read — a USB-C flash drive plugs straight into a modern Asus phone, or a regular USB drive with a USB-C OTG adapter; older Asus phones with a Micro-USB port need a Micro-USB OTG adapter instead; enough space on the drive for the photos you want to keep. Three Asus specifics: first, there is no OTG switch to hunt for. Asus phones run ZenUI — close to stock Android on recent models, so the drive mounts on plug-in; look for a "USB storage added" or "USB drive connected" notification; if the phone ignores the drive, check Settings > Storage; no documented Asus OTG switch location was found, and whether a switch exists at all is unverified — so don't assume a missing switch means a broken phone; not every Asus phone has OTG at all — the original Zenfone 5 and the Zenfone 2 don't, while the Zenfone 3 Laser, Zenfone 4, Zenfone 6, and Zenfone 7 Pro do — so for any other model check its specs. Second, Asus's stock file manager is File Manager (ZenUI File Manager), which handles the phone's internal storage and its connected external storage, and the stock gallery is Asus Gallery — on Zenfone 9 and 10 you cannot even set Google Photos as the default gallery — and Asus camera photos live in DCIM/Camera — and whether your model has a microSD slot varies by model (the Zenfone 7 Pro takes one up to 2 TB), so check your own model's specs rather than assuming one either way; a USB drive is the plug-in storage that works on every model. Third, Asus phones ship with Google Play, so SnapDisk installs from the v0.1.2 APK on the GitHub release page today and from Play once the listing is live — there is no sideload-only situation here. One format note: drives formatted FAT32 can't hold a single file over 4 GB; that only matters for very long videos — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup; a drive formatted exFAT has no such limit.

Method 3: Asus's own tools (Phone Clone, Google backup, or the cloud — not phone-to-USB). If you want Asus's own route, know what each tool actually does — none of them writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive. ASUS Phone Clone (formerly ASUS Data Transfer) is Asus's official migration app: it moves contacts, call logs, messages, photos, videos, music, files, and apps from an old Android phone to a new Asus phone over Wi-Fi, with no cable and no mobile network. It is a real transfer tool, and it is the closest Asus's own tools come to this article's job — but it moves your photos to a new phone, not to a USB drive, and Asus's own FAQ says stock-AOSP Zenfones (Max Pro, Max Pro M2, Live L1, Live L2) are not supported at all. Google backup is the other route Asus's guides point to: Settings > System > Backup, Back up to Google Drive on — it backs the phone up to your Google account so you can restore app settings and data to a new Asus phone. It is a real backup — but the backup lives in Google's cloud and restores to a phone, not a folder of photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open. Asus WebStorage is Asus's own cloud — 5 GB free with older Zenfones — and it has the same limit: it backs the phone up to Asus's servers, not to a USB drive. Google Photos is Google's own photo backup app: it automatically backs up photos to Google's cloud, with 15 GB free with every Google account — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and photos sync through Google Photos instead. All of them work fine for what they are. Their limit, for photos specifically: none of them gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open.

What this does not do: photos and videos only (SnapDisk copies image and video files; documents, voice notes, and anything that isn't a photo or video is skipped — Google backup is the tool if you want contacts, messages, and settings in the same backup, not just photos); only the folder you pick (by default DCIM — your camera photos; photos in other folders only copy if you point the From folder at them, or at a parent folder that contains them); free 5 GB per run (a library bigger than 5 GB stops at the cap; run it again and it picks up where it stopped; Pro, $9.99 one-time, removes the limit and starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk); files over 4 GB on FAT32 are skipped (very long videos on a FAT32 drive are listed with their reason instead of failing the backup — reformat the drive to exFAT if you need them); it never deletes (SnapDisk only copies — freeing space on the phone is copy, check the copy on the drive, then delete the originals yourself, never the other way round).

What to avoid: hunting for an OTG switch that may not exist (no documented Asus OTG switch location was found, and ZenUI mounts the drive on plug-in with a "USB storage added" notification; if your Asus phone ignores a drive, check Settings > Storage — but a missing switch is not proof the phone is broken; not every Asus phone has OTG at all; the original Zenfone 5 and the Zenfone 2 don't; for any other model, check its specs); mistaking a phone-to-phone move for a photo copy (ASUS Phone Clone moves your photos to a new Asus phone — if you want to plug the drive into a computer and open the pictures, you need a plain copy, that is Method 1 or 2, not Phone Clone); mistaking a cloud backup for a photo copy (Google backup, Asus WebStorage, and Google Photos back your phone up to Google's or Asus's servers — if you want to plug the drive into a computer and open the pictures, you need a plain copy, that is Method 1 or 2, not a cloud backup); PC-only tools when you have no computer (drag-and-drop through a Windows PC works — but it needs the PC in between; if the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route); cloud backup dressed as USB backup (if the app needs an account and an upload before your photos are safe, that's a cloud subscription with a USB step; on Asus the cloud routes are Google Photos, Google One, and Asus WebStorage — and Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, which is the one place quality actually gets lost); deleting before verifying (copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round; SnapDisk only copies, it never deletes, so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check); moving instead of copying (the file manager's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step — if the copy fails halfway, photos are already gone from the phone; copy first, verify, then delete); unplugging mid-copy (pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight — wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first — SnapDisk's Stop button exists for exactly this).

### Back up Infinix photos to a USB drive (no computer)

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/infinix-photos-to-usb.html

Infinix phones (Note, Hot, Zero, and GT series) run XOS — Infinix's Android skin — with OTG support that varies by model: most recent models mount the drive on plug-in with a "USB storage added" notification, but some budget models have no OTG at all. And Infinix's own backup tools back your photos up to the cloud or to a PC, not to a USB drive as plain files. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into a modern Infinix. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

TL;DR: On an Infinix phone, check your model supports OTG first — the Note 12 G96, Zero 30 5G, and Hot 70 do, but the Smart 5 has no OTG at all, so no adapter will make a drive appear on it — then plug a USB drive in: most OTG models mount it straight away with a "USB storage added" notification; if nothing appears, check Settings > Storage (one guide reports an OTG toggle at Settings > More Connections on the Zero 30, but that report is AI-generated and unverified, so treat the location as a lead, not a fact) — then tap Backup in SnapDisk, and your whole photo library copies oldest-first to the drive in the background — with real progress (percent, GB copied / total, speed, time left), Pause and Stop, and resume where it stopped if you unplug. No computer, no upload, no account. The copies are the original files: SnapDisk streams each file byte-for-byte to the drive, never recompresses or resizes, and checks the size of every file after copying. The honest contrast, up front: Infinix File Manager works — it is the stock file manager on Infinix phones, and it copies photos to a USB drive — but it is manual select-copy-paste with no progress detail, no resume, and no verification; Infinix's own backup routes work too, but none of them writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive — Google backup restores your data to a new phone from the cloud, XCloud backs photos up to Infinix's cloud, Coolmuster backs the phone up to a PC, and the SD-card route copies to a card, not a drive. One rival app does exist — Photos to USB: OTG Backup copies a whole gallery to a pen drive in one tap and resumes where it stopped — so SnapDisk is not the only one-tap option; what it adds is oldest-first order, detailed progress with Pause and Stop, size verification of every file, no ads, and a free 5 GB per run with a $9.99 one-time Pro for auto-backup and unlimited size. SnapDisk copies, it never deletes — deleting from the phone afterwards is your step, only after verifying a few photos on the drive. Free version: 5 GB per run; run it again past the cap and it picks up where it stopped, because files already copied are never copied twice. As of November 17, 2026, no top search result for this query is an Infinix-specific guide at all, let alone an Infinix-specific automated whole-library backup with progress, Pause/Stop, and resume: the top results are generic manual guides, PC tools, or a rival app page.

Mascom's Hot 70 listing (mascomintl.com) — a retailer spec page for the Hot 70 (released May 2026) that lists "USB-C with OTG — read flash drives directly to share files, music or presentations without a laptop in between", plus a dedicated microSDXC slot that takes a memory card while both SIM slots stay in use; a third model with confirmed OTG, from its spec sheet. FoneArena's GT 50 Pro unboxing (fonearena.com/blog/497019/infinix-gt-50-pro-unboxing-first-impressions.html) — the newest Infinix runs Android 16 with XOS 16 on top, with a USB Type-C port on the bottom; XOS 16 is the current skin; the page does not state OTG support for this model, so don't assume it — check the specs. 91mobiles' XOS 16 hands-on (91mobiles.com/reviews/infinix-xos-16-hands/amp/) — XOS 16 redesigned the first-party apps, including Gallery and File Manager, and the Gallery app gained AI imaging features (AI Flare Remover, AI Shadow Remover, AI Reflection Remover); the stock gallery and file manager on a current Infinix are XOS's own Gallery and File Manager apps. XOS's stock apps (toolify.ai and nairaland.com) — the stock gallery on Infinix phones is AI Gallery, in the box since XOS 5.5, and the stock file manager is File Manager, which browses internal storage and external memory cards; both are XOS's own apps, not Google's — though Google Photos is also on the phone for cloud backup. Cloud routes — Google Photos backs up over Wi-Fi to Google's servers, not to a drive you hold; its "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, and a cloud backup stops working the day you stop paying for storage. Infinix's own cloud is XCloud — it backs the phone up to Infinix's servers, not to a USB drive — and it is not on every model: one guide says newer Infinix phones with XOS above 7 usually have it, so check your own phone before counting on it. None of them is an Infinix-specific guide at all, and none of them offers an automated Infinix photo-library backup: nothing that takes the entire camera roll, copies it oldest-first in the background as plain files you can open anywhere, shows progress, pauses and resumes, and verifies every file.

What you need: an Infinix phone (Android 7.0 or later for SnapDisk) that supports OTG — check your model's specs before buying anything; a USB drive your phone can read — a USB-C flash drive plugs straight into a modern Infinix, or a regular USB drive with a USB-C OTG adapter; older Infinix phones with a Micro-USB port need a Micro-USB OTG adapter instead; enough space on the drive for the photos you want to keep. Three Infinix specifics: first, OTG is not a given. Infinix phones run XOS — Infinix's Android skin — and the drive mounts on plug-in on models that support OTG; look for a "USB storage added" or "USB drive connected" notification; one guide reports an OTG toggle at Settings > More Connections on the Zero 30, and that Infinix turns OTG off after 10 minutes with nothing connected — but that report is AI-generated and unverified, and it warns itself that firmware versions can move the toggle, so treat the path as a lead to check, not a fact; if the phone ignores the drive, check Settings > Storage; and not every Infinix phone has OTG at all — the Smart 5 doesn't, while the Note 12 G96, Zero 30 5G, and Hot 70 do — so for any other model check its specs, and don't assume a missing toggle means a broken phone. Second, Infinix's stock file manager is File Manager, which handles the phone's internal storage and connected external storage, and the stock gallery is AI Gallery — and Infinix camera photos live in DCIM/Camera — and whether your model has a microSD slot varies by model (the Hot 70 has a dedicated microSD slot), so check your own model's specs rather than assuming one either way; a USB drive is the plug-in storage that works on every OTG model. Third, Infinix phones ship with Google Play, so SnapDisk installs from the v0.1.2 APK on the GitHub release page today and from Play once the listing is live — there is no sideload-only situation here. One format note: drives formatted FAT32 can't hold a single file over 4 GB; that only matters for very long videos — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup; a drive formatted exFAT has no such limit.

Method 3: Infinix's own tools (Google backup, XCloud, or a PC — not phone-to-USB). If you want Infinix's own route, know what each tool actually does — none of them writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive. Google backup is the route Infinix's guides point to first: Settings > Google > Backup, Back up to Google Drive on — it backs the phone up to your Google account so you can restore app settings and data to a new phone. It is a real backup — but the backup lives in Google's cloud and restores to a phone, not a folder of photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open. XCloud is Infinix's own cloud backup, on phones that have it: Settings > System > Backup & Reset, Local Backup or XCloud Backup — it backs contacts, messages, photos, and settings up to your Infinix account. It is a real backup too — but it lives on Infinix's servers, needs an Infinix account and a connection, and is not on every model (one guide says newer phones with XOS above 7 usually have it), and it still doesn't give you a folder of photo files on a USB drive. Google Photos is Google's own photo backup app: it automatically backs up photos to Google's cloud, with 15 GB free with every Google account — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and photos sync through Google Photos instead. Coolmuster Android Backup Manager is the PC route the Infinix guides offer: a Windows tool that backs the whole phone up to a computer in one click — but it needs the computer, a USB cable, and USB debugging on. And the SD-card route copies DCIM to a memory card with File Manager — a real local copy, but it stays on a card in the phone (or needs a card reader to open anywhere else), not a USB drive you can plug into any computer. All of them work fine for what they are. Their limit, for photos specifically: none of them gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open.

What this does not do: photos and videos only (SnapDisk copies image and video files; documents, voice notes, and anything that isn't a photo or video is skipped — Google backup is the tool if you want contacts, messages, and settings in the same backup, not just photos); only the folder you pick (by default DCIM — your camera photos; photos in other folders only copy if you point the From folder at them, or at a parent folder that contains them); free 5 GB per run (a library bigger than 5 GB stops at the cap; run it again and it picks up where it stopped; Pro, $9.99 one-time, removes the limit and starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk); files over 4 GB on FAT32 are skipped (very long videos on a FAT32 drive are listed with their reason instead of failing the backup — reformat the drive to exFAT if you need them); it never deletes (SnapDisk only copies — freeing space on the phone is copy, check the copy on the drive, then delete the originals yourself, never the other way round); no OTG, no USB backup (on a model without OTG — the Smart 5 is the confirmed one — a USB drive simply never appears, and no app can change that; the cloud routes, Google Photos and XCloud, are the backup for those phones).

What to avoid: buying an adapter before checking OTG (not every Infinix phone has OTG — the Smart 5 doesn't, and no adapter or setting can enable it; check your own model's specs first, or the drive will never appear no matter what you plug in); hunting for an OTG switch that may not exist (one guide reports a toggle at Settings > More Connections on the Zero 30, but that report is AI-generated and unverified, and XOS mounts the drive on plug-in with a "USB storage added" notification on models that support OTG; if your Infinix phone ignores a drive, check Settings > Storage — but a missing switch is not proof the phone is broken; some models simply have no OTG); mistaking a cloud backup for a photo copy (Google backup, XCloud, and Google Photos back your phone up to Google's or Infinix's servers — if you want to plug the drive into a computer and open the pictures, you need a plain copy, that is Method 1 or 2, not a cloud backup); mistaking a PC tool for a phone-to-USB copy (Coolmuster backs the phone up to a computer — it needs the PC, a cable, and USB debugging; if the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route, not a desktop tool); mistaking an SD-card copy for a USB backup (copying DCIM to a memory card is a real local copy — but the card stays in the phone, and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader; a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is); PC-only tools when you have no computer (drag-and-drop through a Windows PC works — but it needs the PC in between; if the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route); cloud backup dressed as USB backup (if the app needs an account and an upload before your photos are safe, that's a cloud subscription with a USB step; on Infinix the cloud routes are Google Photos, Google One, and XCloud — and Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, which is the one place quality actually gets lost); deleting before verifying (copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round; SnapDisk only copies, it never deletes, so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check); moving instead of copying (the file manager's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step — if the copy fails halfway, photos are already gone from the phone; copy first, verify, then delete); unplugging mid-copy (pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight — wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first — SnapDisk's Stop button exists for exactly this).

### Back up Tecno photos to a USB drive (no computer)

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/tecno-photos-to-usb.html

Tecno phones (Spark, Camon, Pova, Phantom, and Pop series) run HiOS — Tecno's Android skin — with OTG support that varies by model: most recent models mount the drive on plug-in with a "USB storage added" notification, but support is not universal, and some older models list OTG in the specs without it working out of the box. And Tecno's own backup tools back your photos up to the cloud, to an SD card, or to a PC, not to a USB drive as plain files. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into a modern Tecno. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

TL;DR: On a Tecno phone, check your model supports OTG first — Tecno's official spec pages list OTG for the POP 7 Pro, CAMON 20 Pro, POVA 7, and SPARK Go 2024, and spec tables list it for the Pova 5 Pro too — but support varies by model and regional variant, so check your own model's specs, and don't assume a missing toggle means a broken phone: the Pop 3 lists OTG in its specs, but owners report it not enabled out of the box — then plug a USB drive in: most OTG models mount it straight away with a "USB storage added" notification; if nothing appears, check Settings > Storage (one low-quality guide reports an OTG toggle in the connection settings on the Pova 4, but that report is unverified, so treat the location as a lead, not a fact) — then tap Backup in SnapDisk, and your whole photo library copies oldest-first to the drive in the background — with real progress (percent, GB copied / total, speed, time left), Pause and Stop, and resume where it stopped if you unplug. No computer, no upload, no account. The copies are the original files: SnapDisk streams each file byte-for-byte to the drive, never recompresses or resizes, and checks the size of every file after copying. The honest contrast, up front: Tecno's File Manager works — it is Transsion's file manager, the stock file manager on Tecno phones, and it copies photos to a USB drive — but it is manual select-copy-paste with no progress detail, no resume, and no verification; Tecno's own backup routes work too, but none of them writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive — Google backup restores your data to a new phone from the cloud, TECNO Cloud backs photos up to Tecno's cloud, the built-in Backup & Restore writes to the phone or an SD card, and Coolmuster backs the phone up to a PC. One rival app does exist — Photos to USB: OTG Backup copies a whole gallery to a pen drive in one tap and resumes where it stopped — so SnapDisk is not the only one-tap option; what it adds is oldest-first order, detailed progress with Pause and Stop, size verification of every file, no ads, and a free 5 GB per run with a $9.99 one-time Pro for auto-backup and unlimited size. SnapDisk copies, it never deletes — deleting from the phone afterwards is your step, only after verifying a few photos on the drive. Free version: 5 GB per run; run it again past the cap and it picks up where it stopped, because files already copied are never copied twice. Google Photos (Play listing, com.google.android.apps.photos) — Google's own photo backup: 15 GB of cloud storage free with every Google account, automatic upload over Wi-Fi; cloud, not a USB copy. Transsion File Manager (Play listing, com.transsion.filemanagerx) — the stock file manager on Tecno phones, by Shanghai Transsion Co., Ltd.: a file manager with category browsing by music, video, image, document, zip, and apk, plus global search; this is the File Manager app the manual method uses. PakObserver's Google AI Plus story (pakobserver.net/tecno-makes-everyday-smartphone-use-easier-with-free-2tb-cloud-storage/) — eligible Tecno smartphones launched from December 2025 come with three months of Google AI Plus, including 2TB of cloud storage for automatic backups; a cloud offer for newer Tecno phones — generous, but it is still a cloud backup, not a folder of photo files on a USB drive. Cloud routes — Google Photos backs up over Wi-Fi to Google's servers, not to a drive you hold; its "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, and a cloud backup stops working the day you stop paying for storage. Tecno's own cloud is TECNO Cloud, also called HiOS Cloud — it backs the phone up to Tecno's servers, not to a USB drive — and it needs a TECNO account and a connection, so check your own phone before counting on it. None of them is a Tecno-specific guide at all, and none of them offers an automated Tecno photo-library backup: nothing that takes the entire camera roll, copies it oldest-first in the background as plain files you can open anywhere, shows progress, pauses and resumes, and verifies every file.

What you need: a Tecno phone (Android 7.0 or later for SnapDisk) that supports OTG — check your model's specs before buying anything; a USB drive your phone can read — a USB-C flash drive plugs straight into a modern Tecno, or a regular USB drive with a USB-C OTG adapter; older Tecno phones with a Micro-USB port need a Micro-USB OTG adapter instead; enough space on the drive for the photos you want to keep. Three Tecno specifics: first, OTG is not a given. Tecno phones run HiOS — Tecno's Android skin — and the drive mounts on plug-in on models that support OTG; look for a "USB storage added" or "USB drive connected" notification; one low-quality guide reports an OTG toggle in the connection settings on the Pova 4 — but that report is unverified, so treat the path as a lead to check, not a fact; if the phone ignores the drive, check Settings > Storage; and not every Tecno phone has OTG working out of the box — the Pop 3 lists it in the specs while owners report it not enabled — so for any other model check its specs, and don't assume a missing toggle means a broken phone. Second, Tecno's stock file manager is File Manager, Transsion's file manager, which handles the phone's internal storage and connected external storage — and Tecno camera photos live in DCIM/Camera — and whether your model has a microSD slot varies by model, so check your own model's specs rather than assuming one either way; a USB drive is the plug-in storage that works on every OTG model. Third, Tecno phones ship with Google Play, so SnapDisk installs from the v0.1.2 APK on the GitHub release page today and from Play once the listing is live — there is no sideload-only situation here. One format note: drives formatted FAT32 can't hold a single file over 4 GB; that only matters for very long videos — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup; a drive formatted exFAT has no such limit.

Method 3: Tecno's own tools (built-in backup, TECNO Cloud, Google backup, or a PC — not phone-to-USB). If you want Tecno's own route, know what each tool actually does — none of them writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive. The built-in Backup & Restore is the offline route: Settings > System > Back up & reset, Local backup or Phone backup — it backs contacts, messages, call logs, system data, and apps to the phone's internal storage or an SD card, with no computer and no internet. It is a real backup — but it writes to the phone or a card, not to a USB drive, and the menu names come from a third-party tool vendor's guide, not Tecno's own site, so check them on your own phone. TECNO Cloud is Tecno's own cloud backup, also called HiOS Cloud: Settings > TECNO Cloud, sign in with a TECNO account, choose Backup, pick the data types, Back up now — it backs contacts, photos, messages, and app settings up to Tecno's servers and restores them on any Tecno device. It is a real backup too — but it lives on Tecno's servers, needs a TECNO account and a connection, and it still doesn't give you a folder of photo files on a USB drive. Google backup is the route Tecno's guides point to first: Settings > Google > Backup, Back up by Google One on — it backs the phone up to your Google account so you can restore app settings and data to a new phone. It is a real backup — but the backup lives in Google's cloud and restores to a phone, not a folder of photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open. Google Photos is Google's own photo backup app: it automatically backs up photos to Google's cloud, with 15 GB free with every Google account — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and photos sync through Google Photos instead. Eligible Tecno phones launched from December 2025 also get three months of Google AI Plus with 2TB of cloud storage — generous, but still a cloud backup. Coolmuster Android Backup Manager is the PC route the Tecno guides offer: a Windows tool that backs the whole phone up to a computer in one click — but it needs the computer, a USB cable, and USB debugging on. And the SD-card route copies DCIM to a memory card with File Manager — a real local copy, but it stays on a card in the phone (or needs a card reader to open anywhere else), not a USB drive you can plug into any computer. All of them work fine for what they are. Their limit, for photos specifically: none of them gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open.

What this does not do: photos and videos only (SnapDisk copies image and video files; documents, voice notes, and anything that isn't a photo or video is skipped — Google backup is the tool if you want contacts, messages, and settings in the same backup, not just photos); only the folder you pick (by default DCIM — your camera photos; photos in other folders only copy if you point the From folder at them, or at a parent folder that contains them); free 5 GB per run (a library bigger than 5 GB stops at the cap; run it again and it picks up where it stopped; Pro, $9.99 one-time, removes the limit and starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk); files over 4 GB on FAT32 are skipped (very long videos on a FAT32 drive are listed with their reason instead of failing the backup — reformat the drive to exFAT if you need them); it never deletes (SnapDisk only copies — freeing space on the phone is copy, check the copy on the drive, then delete the originals yourself, never the other way round); no OTG, no USB backup (on a model without working OTG — the Pop 3 lists it in the specs while owners report it not enabled — a USB drive may simply never appear, and no app can change that; the cloud routes, Google Photos and TECNO Cloud, are the backup for those phones).

What to avoid: buying an adapter before checking OTG (not every Tecno phone has working OTG — the Pop 3 lists it in the specs while owners report it not enabled; check your own model's specs first, or the drive will never appear no matter what you plug in); hunting for an OTG switch that may not exist (one guide reports a toggle in the connection settings on the Pova 4, but that report is unverified, and HiOS mounts the drive on plug-in with a "USB storage added" notification on models that support OTG; if your Tecno phone ignores a drive, check Settings > Storage — but a missing switch is not proof the phone is broken; some models simply have no working OTG); mistaking a cloud backup for a photo copy (Google backup, TECNO Cloud, and Google Photos back your phone up to Google's or Tecno's servers — if you want to plug the drive into a computer and open the pictures, you need a plain copy, that is Method 1 or 2, not a cloud backup); mistaking a PC tool for a phone-to-USB copy (Coolmuster backs the phone up to a computer — it needs the PC, a cable, and USB debugging; if the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route, not a desktop tool); mistaking an SD-card copy for a USB backup (copying DCIM to a memory card is a real local copy — but the card stays in the phone, and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader; a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is); PC-only tools when you have no computer (drag-and-drop through a Windows PC works — but it needs the PC in between; if the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route); cloud backup dressed as USB backup (if the app needs an account and an upload before your photos are safe, that's a cloud subscription with a USB step; on Tecno the cloud routes are Google Photos, Google One, and TECNO Cloud — and Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, which is the one place quality actually gets lost); deleting before verifying (copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round; SnapDisk only copies, it never deletes, so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check); moving instead of copying (the file manager's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step — if the copy fails halfway, photos are already gone from the phone; copy first, verify, then delete); unplugging mid-copy (pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight — wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first — SnapDisk's Stop button exists for exactly this).

Files by Google (Play listing, com.google.android.apps.nbu.files) — Google's file manager: browse files, see how much space is left on the device, SD card and USB drive, and move files to Google Drive or an SD card; this is the Files app the manual method uses — Nothing OS ships Google's apps rather than its own file manager. Nothing Community thread (nothing.community/d/4803-nothing-please-do-not-create-your-version-system-apps/9) — Nothing Phone 2 owners in the community describe the stock setup as Google's apps: Dialler, Contacts, Messages, Gallery, and Files; a user thread, not an official statement — but it matches the near-stock Nothing OS setup, and it is the basis for naming Files by Google as the stock file manager here. gadgetsfocus OTG fixes (gadgetsfocus.com/phone-not-reading-usb-flash-drive-ssd-otg-fixes/) — a general OTG troubleshooting guide: file system, power limits, and the OTG toggle on OnePlus, OPPO, Realme, and Vivo phones; useful background, not a Nothing guide — and its toggle advice is for other brands, not Nothing. AnExplorer's OTG troubleshooting (anexplorer.io/solve/cant-access-usb) — a general guide to a drive not appearing: wrong or charge-only adapter, incompatible file system, or missing storage permission; useful background, not a Nothing guide. Photos to USB: OTG Backup (Play listing, com.arzdrz.photos_to_usb) — the one-tap app alternative, from the wider search for this job: a real phone-to-USB app that copies the whole gallery to a pen drive in one tap, copies only new photos next time, and warns about the FAT32 4 GB limit; free with ads, with a one-time purchase to remove them. It is the closest thing to this article's job — but it is a generic Android listing, not a Nothing guide, and it does not promise oldest-first order, detailed progress with Pause and Stop, or size verification of every file. Google Photos (Play listing, com.google.android.apps.photos) — Google's own photo backup: 15 GB of cloud storage free with every Google account, automatic upload over Wi-Fi; cloud, not a USB copy. Cloud routes — Google Photos backs up over Wi-Fi to Google's servers, not to a drive you hold; its "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, and a cloud backup stops working the day you stop paying for storage. Nothing has no own cloud backup for photos — the backup routes on a Nothing phone are Google's — so check your own phone before counting on anything else. None of them is a Nothing-specific guide at all, and none of them offers an automated Nothing photo-library backup: nothing that takes the entire camera roll, copies it oldest-first in the background as plain files you can open anywhere, shows progress, pauses and resumes, and verifies every file.

What you need: a Nothing phone (Android 7.0 or later for SnapDisk) that supports OTG — check your model's specs before buying anything; a USB drive your phone can read — a USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any Nothing phone, or a regular USB drive with a USB-C OTG adapter; enough space on the drive for the photos you want to keep. Three Nothing specifics: first, OTG is not a given on every model. Nothing phones run Nothing OS — a near-stock Android skin — and the drive mounts on plug-in on models that support OTG; look for a "USB storage added" or "USB drive connected" notification. Spec tables list OTG for the Phone (1), Phone (2), Phone (2a), Phone (2a) Plus, and Phone (3a) — but the CMF Phone 1 is disputed: GSMArena lists its USB as Type-C with no OTG, one comparison site lists OTG as not supported, and another lists it as supported — so check your own phone before buying an adapter. If the phone ignores the drive, check Settings > Storage. Second, Nothing OS ships Google's apps, so the stock file manager is Files by Google, which handles the phone's internal storage and connected external storage — and Nothing camera photos live in DCIM/Camera — and only the CMF Phone 1 has a microSD slot; the main Phone models have none, so a USB drive is the plug-in storage for them. Third, Nothing phones ship with Google Play, so SnapDisk installs from the v0.1.2 APK on the GitHub release page today and from Play once the listing is live — there is no sideload-only situation here. One format note: drives formatted FAT32 can't hold a single file over 4 GB; that only matters for very long videos — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup; a drive formatted exFAT has no such limit.

Method 3: Nothing's own tools (Google Photos and Google backup — not phone-to-USB). If you want Nothing's own route, know what each tool actually does — Nothing has no own cloud backup for photos; the routes on a Nothing phone are Google's, and none of them writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive. Google Photos is Google's own photo backup app, and the gallery app on Nothing OS 2.x: open Photos, tap your profile picture, Photos settings, Backup, and turn Backup on — it automatically backs up photos to your Google account, with 15 GB free with every Google account. On Nothing OS 3.0 and later the gallery app is Nothing Gallery instead — a clean media viewer for photos and videos, not a backup tool — and Google Photos is still the backup route. Either way it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and photos sync through Google Photos instead. Google backup is the route Nothing's guides point to first: Settings > Google > Backup, Back up by Google One on — it backs the phone up to your Google account so you can restore app settings and data to a new phone. It is a real backup — but the backup lives in Google's cloud and restores to a phone, not a folder of photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open. And the SD-card route copies DCIM to a memory card with Files — a real local copy, but only the CMF Phone 1 has a microSD slot, and the card stays in the phone (or needs a card reader to open anywhere else), not a USB drive you can plug into any computer. All of them work fine for what they are. Their limit, for photos specifically: none of them gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open. If what you want is a copy of your photos you can open anywhere, Method 1 or 2 is the route.

What this does not do: photos and videos only (SnapDisk copies image and video files; documents, voice notes, and anything that isn't a photo or video is skipped — Google backup is the tool if you want contacts, messages, and settings in the same backup, not just photos); only the folder you pick (by default DCIM — your camera photos; photos in other folders only copy if you point the From folder at them, or at a parent folder that contains them); free 5 GB per run (a library bigger than 5 GB stops at the cap; run it again and it picks up where it stopped; Pro, $9.99 one-time, removes the limit and starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk); files over 4 GB on FAT32 are skipped (very long videos on a FAT32 drive are listed with their reason instead of failing the backup — reformat the drive to exFAT if you need them); it never deletes (SnapDisk only copies — freeing space on the phone is copy, check the copy on the drive, then delete the originals yourself, never the other way round); no OTG, no USB backup (on a model without working OTG — the CMF Phone 1's OTG support is unconfirmed, with spec tables disagreeing — a USB drive simply never appears, and no app can change that; the cloud routes, Google Photos and Google backup, are the backup for those phones).

What to avoid: buying an adapter before checking OTG (not every Nothing phone is confirmed to have OTG — the CMF Phone 1's OTG support is disputed between spec tables; check your own model's specs first, or the drive will never appear no matter what you plug in); hunting for an OTG switch that does not exist (Nothing OS mounts the drive on plug-in with a "USB storage added" notification on models that support OTG — there is no OTG toggle to turn on; the toggle advice in general OTG guides is for OnePlus, OPPO, Realme, and Vivo phones, not Nothing; if your Nothing phone ignores a drive, check Settings > Storage — but a missing switch is not proof the phone is broken; some models simply have no working OTG); mistaking a cloud backup for a photo copy (Google backup and Google Photos back your phone up to Google's servers — if you want to plug the drive into a computer and open the pictures, you need a plain copy, that is Method 1 or 2, not a cloud backup); mistaking a PC tool for a phone-to-USB copy (drag-and-drop through a computer works — but it needs the PC in between; if the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route, not a desktop tool); mistaking an SD-card copy for a USB backup (copying DCIM to a memory card is a real local copy — but only the CMF Phone 1 has a microSD slot, the card stays in the phone, and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader; a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is); PC-only tools when you have no computer (drag-and-drop through a Windows PC works — but it needs the PC in between; if the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route); cloud backup dressed as USB backup (if the app needs an account and an upload before your photos are safe, that's a cloud subscription with a USB step; on Nothing the cloud routes are Google Photos and Google backup — and Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, which is the one place quality actually gets lost); deleting before verifying (copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round; SnapDisk only copies, it never deletes, so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check); moving instead of copying (the file manager's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step — if the copy fails halfway, photos are already gone from the phone; copy first, verify, then delete); unplugging mid-copy (pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight — wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first — SnapDisk's Stop button exists for exactly this).

### Back up POCO photos to a USB drive (no computer)

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/poco-photos-to-usb.html

POCO phones (F, X, and M series) run HyperOS — Xiaomi's Android skin, since POCO is Xiaomi's sub-brand — with OTG support on the F and X series: spec tables list USB Type-C 2.0 with OTG for the F7, F7 Pro, X7, and X7 Pro, and USB Type-C 3.2 with OTG for the F9 Ultra — but the budget M series is the exception to check, because spec tables disagree on whether the M7 supports OTG at all. And POCO's own backup tools are Xiaomi Cloud and Google's — Google Photos and Google backup — which back your photos up to the cloud, not to a USB drive as plain files. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any POCO phone. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

TL;DR: On a POCO phone, enable OTG first — on many HyperOS phones it is off by default, so go to Settings > Additional settings > OTG (on some phones the switch is under More settings > OTG) and turn it on, with the drive already attached, because the switch turns itself off again after about 10 minutes without a drive — then plug a USB drive in: OTG models mount it straight away with a "USB storage added" notification; if nothing appears, check Settings > Storage — then tap Backup in SnapDisk, and your whole photo library copies oldest-first to the drive in the background — with real progress (percent, GB copied / total, speed, time left), Pause and Stop, and resume where it stopped if you unplug. No computer, no upload, no account. The copies are the original files: SnapDisk streams each file byte-for-byte to the drive, never recompresses or resizes, and checks the size of every file after copying. The honest contrast, up front: Mi File Manager works — it is the stock file manager on POCO phones, and it copies photos to a USB drive — but it is manual select-copy-paste with no progress detail, no resume, and no verification, and it shows banner ads while you browse your own files; POCO's own backup routes work too, but they are Xiaomi Cloud and Google's routes — Xiaomi Cloud, Google Photos, and Google backup — and none of them writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive: Xiaomi Cloud syncs your gallery to Xiaomi's servers, Google Photos backs photos up to Google's cloud, and Google backup restores your data to a new phone from the cloud. One rival app does exist — Photos to USB: OTG Backup copies a whole gallery to a pen drive in one tap and resumes where it stopped — so SnapDisk is not the only one-tap option; what it adds is oldest-first order, detailed progress with Pause and Stop, size verification of every file, no ads, and a free 5 GB per run with a $9.99 one-time Pro for auto-backup and unlimited size. SnapDisk copies, it never deletes — deleting from the phone afterwards is your step, only after verifying a few photos on the drive. Free version: 5 GB per run; run it again past the cap and it picks up where it stopped, because files already copied are never copied twice. It backs your photos up to Xiaomi's servers and restores them on another Xiaomi, Redmi, or POCO phone. It is a real backup — but it lives on Xiaomi's servers, needs a Xiaomi account and a connection, its free storage is limited so a large photo library needs a paid plan, and it still doesn't give you a folder of photo files on a USB drive. Your POCO's default gallery app is Xiaomi Gallery, not Google Photos — Google Photos integrates with it through the default-gallery access feature, so backed-up photos show up in the gallery — but either way it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and photos sync through Google Photos instead. Google backup is the route Xiaomi's guides point to first: Settings > Google > Backup, Back up by Google One on — it backs the phone up to your Google account so you can restore app settings and data to a new phone. It is a real backup — but the backup lives in Google's cloud and restores to a phone, not a folder of photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open. SnapDisk copies, it never deletes — deleting from the phone afterwards is your step, only after verifying a few photos on the drive. Free version: 5 GB per run; run it again past the cap and it picks up where it stopped, because files already copied are never copied twice. As of November 17, 2026, no top search result for this query is a Redmi-specific guide at all, let alone a Redmi-specific automated whole-library backup with progress, Pause/Stop, and resume: the top results are generic manual guides, PC tools, or rival app pages.

What the search results actually offer: search "back up Redmi photos to USB drive without computer" and there is no Redmi-specific result in the top results at all — the rest are generic Android guides, in different packaging. Dr.Fone (drfone.wondershare.com/android-transfer/how-to-transfer-photos-from-android-to-usb.html) — OTG copy, PC drag-and-drop, Google Drive, or AirDroid over Wi-Fi; generic Android, and most of the ways need a computer or a cloud account. AnExplorer (anexplorer.io/transfer/phone-to-usb) — connect the drive with an OTG adapter, open AnExplorer, long-press to select files in DCIM/Camera, Copy, Paste to the drive: a thorough manual guide, and the only one of these guides that shows a progress bar with speed and time remaining — but it is still a manual copy, with no resume or verification. Coolmuster (coolmuster.com/android/transfer-files-from-android-to-usb-flash-drive.html) — OTG copy, a PC tool, or a cloud service; generic Android, and two of the three ways need a computer. AnExplorer's Xiaomi device page (anexplorer.io/device/phone/xiaomi) — a file-manager comparison page for Xiaomi, Redmi, and POCO phones: Xiaomi's built-in File Manager (part of MIUI/HyperOS) shows banner ads while browsing your own files, and it notes that phones with SD card slots (Redmi Note series, POCO M series) benefit from moving media to the card; a file-manager page, not a backup guide — but it confirms Redmi phones run MIUI/HyperOS with Xiaomi's File Manager built in, and that the Redmi Note series has the SD card slot. File Manager by Xiaomi (Play listing, com.mi.android.globalFileexplorer) — Xiaomi's own file manager: quick search, moving, deleting, opening, renaming, unzipping, and copy-paste; this is the stock file manager the manual method uses — it is Xiaomi's preinstalled file app on global MIUI and HyperOS phones. Xiaomi's HyperOS backup guide (xiaomi-plus.com/how-to-back-up-a-xiaomi-phone-xiaomi-cloud-google-and-local-backup-hyperos/) — the three backup options on a HyperOS phone: Google backup, Xiaomi Cloud, and local backup to a computer with a USB cable; a backup guide for Xiaomi phones running HyperOS — the same system Redmi phones run — but none of its three routes writes plain photo files to a USB drive. Google Photos help (support.google.com/photos/answer/14216276) — Google's default-gallery access feature: let Google Photos share access with your device's default gallery app; Xiaomi is one of the brands that works with this feature — which confirms Xiaomi phones (Redmi included) have their own default gallery app, separate from Google Photos, and Google Photos is the cloud backup behind it. GSMArena's Redmi Note 14 Pro 4G specs (m.gsmarena.com/xiaomi_redmi_note_14_pro_4g_(global)-ampp-13614.php) — USB Type-C 2.0 with OTG, and a microSDXC card slot (uses the shared SIM slot); spec tables, not a guide. GSMArena's Redmi Note 14 Pro 5G specs (m.gsmarena.com/xiaomi_redmi_note_14_pro_5g-ampp-13613.php) — Android 14 with HyperOS, USB Type-C 2.0 with OTG, and no card slot; spec tables, not a guide — and the confirmation that the current Note Pro runs HyperOS with OTG and no microSD slot, so a USB drive is the plug-in storage for it. Photos to USB: OTG Backup (Play listing, com.arzdrz.photos_to_usb) — the one-tap app alternative, from the wider search for this job: a real phone-to-USB app that copies the whole gallery to a pen drive in one tap, copies only new photos next time, and warns about the FAT32 4 GB limit; free with ads, with a one-time purchase to remove them. It is the closest thing to this article's job — but it is a generic Android listing, not a Redmi guide, and it does not promise oldest-first order, detailed progress with Pause and Stop, or size verification of every file. Google Photos (Play listing, com.google.android.apps.photos) — Google's own photo backup: 15 GB of cloud storage free with every Google account, automatic upload over Wi-Fi; cloud, not a USB copy. umatechnology (umatechnology.org/how-to-transfer-photos-from-android-to-a-usb-flash-drive-without-a-computer/) — copy photos with Files by Google or Samsung's My Files, or through a computer as a middleman; notes a photo that exists only in the cloud cannot be copied to a drive until it is downloaded to the phone first; generic Android, not written for Redmi. thegadgetians (thegadgetians.com/how-to-transfer-files-from-phone-to-usb-without-computer/) — OTG adapter plus the phone's file manager for Android, a Lightning adapter for iPhone; generic, and it pushes one maker's photo stick; not a Redmi guide. pixoneye (pixoneye.com/how-to-transfer-photos-from-phone-to-usb-stick/) — copy local originals to compatible USB storage with the phone's file manager, or through a trusted computer; generic Android and iPhone, not written for Redmi. Cloud routes — Xiaomi Cloud syncs your gallery to Xiaomi's servers, Google Photos backs up over Wi-Fi to Google's servers, not to a drive you hold; its "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, and a cloud backup stops working the day you stop paying for storage. Xiaomi Cloud's free storage is limited, so a large photo library needs a paid plan or Google Photos instead. Neither route gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive. None of them is a Redmi-specific guide at all, and none of them offers an automated Redmi photo-library backup: nothing that takes the entire camera roll, copies it oldest-first in the background as plain files you can open anywhere, shows progress, pauses and resumes, and verifies every file.

What you need: a Redmi phone (Android 7.0 or later for SnapDisk) that supports OTG — check your model's specs before buying anything; a USB drive your phone can read — a USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any Redmi phone, or a regular USB drive with a USB-C OTG adapter; enough space on the drive for the photos you want to keep. Three Redmi specifics: first, OTG is not a given on every model, and on many HyperOS phones it is off by default. Redmi phones run HyperOS — Xiaomi's Android skin, since Redmi is Xiaomi's sub-brand — and on many MIUI and HyperOS phones OTG is off unless you enable it in Settings > Additional settings > OTG (on some phones the switch is under More settings > OTG). The switch turns itself off again after about 10 minutes without a drive, so enable it with the drive already attached. On some newer versions there is no OTG switch at all and OTG works directly. Spec tables list USB Type-C 2.0 with OTG for the Note 14 Pro 4G and the Note 14 Pro 5G. If the phone ignores the drive, check Settings > Storage. Second, Redmi ships Xiaomi's apps, so the stock file manager is Mi File Manager — File Manager by Xiaomi, com.mi.android.globalFileexplorer — which handles the phone's internal storage and connected external storage, and shows banner ads while you browse your own files — and Redmi camera photos live in DCIM/Camera — and the microSD slot varies by model: the Note 14 Pro 4G has a microSDXC slot (uses the shared SIM slot) while the Note 14 Pro 5G has none, so a USB drive is the plug-in storage for the 5G model, and check your own model's specs before buying a card. Third, Redmi phones ship with Google Play, so SnapDisk installs from the v0.1.2 APK on the GitHub release page today and from Play once the listing is live — there is no sideload-only situation here. One format note: drives formatted FAT32 can't hold a single file over 4 GB; that only matters for very long videos — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup; a drive formatted exFAT has no such limit.

Method 3: Redmi's own tools (Xiaomi Cloud, Google Photos, and Google backup — not phone-to-USB). If you want Redmi's own route, know what each tool actually does — Redmi has no phone-to-USB backup of its own; the routes on a Redmi phone are Xiaomi Cloud and Google's, and none of them writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive. Xiaomi Cloud is Xiaomi's own cloud backup, and the one Redmi-specific route: open Settings, tap your Xiaomi account at the top, open Xiaomi Cloud, choose what to sync — gallery, contacts, messages, notes, recorder — and use the cloud backup option to save device settings and app data. It backs your photos up to Xiaomi's servers and restores them on another Xiaomi, Redmi, or POCO phone. It is a real backup — but it lives on Xiaomi's servers, needs a Xiaomi account and a connection, its free storage is limited so a large photo library needs a paid plan, and it still doesn't give you a folder of photo files on a USB drive. Google Photos is Google's own photo backup app: open Photos, tap your profile picture, Photos settings, Backup, and turn Backup on — it automatically backs up photos to your Google account, with 15 GB free with every Google account. Your Redmi's default gallery app is Xiaomi Gallery, not Google Photos — Google Photos integrates with it through the default-gallery access feature, so backed-up photos show up in the gallery — but either way it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and photos sync through Google Photos instead. Google backup is the route Xiaomi's guides point to first: Settings > Google > Backup, Back up by Google One on — it backs the phone up to your Google account so you can restore app settings and data to a new phone. It is a real backup — but the backup lives in Google's cloud and restores to a phone, not a folder of photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open. And the SD-card route copies DCIM to a memory card with File Manager — a real local copy, but only some Redmi models have a microSD slot (the Note 14 Pro 4G does, the Note 14 Pro 5G does not), and the card stays in the phone (or needs a card reader to open anywhere else), not a USB drive you can plug into any computer. All of them work fine for what they are. Their limit, for photos specifically: none of them gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open.

What this does not do: photos and videos only (SnapDisk copies image and video files; documents, voice notes, and anything that isn't a photo or video is skipped — Google backup is the tool if you want contacts, messages, and settings in the same backup, not just photos); only the folder you pick (by default DCIM — your camera photos; photos in other folders only copy if you point the From folder at them, or at a parent folder that contains them); free 5 GB per run (a library bigger than 5 GB stops at the cap; run it again and it picks up where it stopped; Pro, $9.99 one-time, removes the limit and starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk); files over 4 GB on FAT32 are skipped (very long videos on a FAT32 drive are listed with their reason instead of failing the backup — reformat the drive to exFAT if you need them); it never deletes (SnapDisk only copies — freeing space on the phone is copy, check the copy on the drive, then delete the originals yourself, never the other way round); no OTG, no USB backup (on a model without working OTG — every Note 14 model in the spec tables lists OTG, but check your own model's specs before buying an adapter — a USB drive may simply never appear, and no app can change that; the cloud routes, Xiaomi Cloud, Google Photos, and Google backup, are the backup for those phones).

What to avoid: buying an adapter before checking OTG (not every Redmi phone is confirmed to have OTG — check your own model's specs first, or the drive will never appear no matter what you plug in); forgetting the OTG switch (on many HyperOS phones OTG is off by default, and the switch turns itself off again after about 10 minutes without a drive — so a drive that worked yesterday can be ignored today; enable it in Settings > Additional settings > OTG with the drive already attached; on some newer versions there is no OTG switch at all and OTG works directly — a missing switch is not proof the phone is broken; some models simply mount the drive on plug-in); mistaking a cloud backup for a photo copy (Xiaomi Cloud, Google backup, and Google Photos back your phone up to Xiaomi's or Google's servers — if you want to plug the drive into a computer and open the pictures, you need a plain copy, that is Method 1 or 2, not a cloud backup); mistaking a PC tool for a phone-to-USB copy (drag-and-drop through a computer works — but it needs the PC in between; if the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route, not a desktop tool); mistaking an SD-card copy for a USB backup (copying DCIM to a memory card is a real local copy — but only some Redmi models have a microSD slot (the Note 14 Pro 4G does, the Note 14 Pro 5G does not), the card stays in the phone, and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader; a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is); PC-only tools when you have no computer (drag-and-drop through a Windows PC works — but it needs the PC in between; if the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route); cloud backup dressed as USB backup (if the app needs an account and an upload before your photos are safe, that's a cloud subscription with a USB step; on Redmi the cloud routes are Xiaomi Cloud, Google Photos, and Google backup — and Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, which is the one place quality actually gets lost); deleting before verifying (copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round; SnapDisk only copies, it never deletes, so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check); moving instead of copying (the file manager's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step — if the copy fails halfway, photos are already gone from the phone; copy first, verify, then delete); unplugging mid-copy (pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight — wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first — SnapDisk's Stop button exists for exactly this).

### SnapDisk FAQ

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/faq.html

The questions a first visitor asks about backing up photos to a USB disk with SnapDisk — answered from how the app actually works in v0.1.2.

TL;DR: SnapDisk backs up your photos to a USB disk — plug it in, tap Backup in the notification, and your photos copy oldest-first in the background, with live progress and Pause / Stop. The free version covers 5 GB per run; Pro is a one-time $9.99 for auto-backup on connect and unlimited size. Nothing is uploaded anywhere: the app has no internet permission, so your photos physically cannot leave your device.

How does SnapDisk back up my photos? Plug in a USB disk and SnapDisk offers a backup in a notification: "External storage is connected. Backup photos?" Tap Backup and your photos and videos copy oldest-first — your earliest photos first — in the background, while you use the phone normally. The progress notification shows real percent, copied / total size, speed, and time left, with Pause and Stop. Every file is size-verified after copying, so the counts are proof, not a promise. Files that already copied are never copied twice.

How much can I back up for free? The free version backs up photos and videos manually, up to 5 GB per backup run, with no ads, no account, and no cloud. SnapDisk Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase (no subscription) that starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk and removes the size limit. There is no subscription and no monthly fee — Pro is paid once.

Does SnapDisk upload my photos anywhere? No. Copying runs entirely on your device, from your internal storage to the external disk you choose. The app has no internet permission, so your photos cannot leave your device. It works with the phone in airplane mode — if a backup works in airplane mode, it is offline, and SnapDisk does.

What happens if I unplug the disk mid-copy? The backup pauses with the full error shown and resumes where it stopped when the disk is back. A partially copied file resumes from where it stopped instead of starting over, and files that already copied are never copied twice. If a file is corrupt or too big for FAT32, it's retried once, then skipped with its reason listed — it never stalls the whole backup.

What disk formats work? Drives formatted exFAT have no per-file size limit. Drives formatted FAT32 can't hold a single file over 4 GB — that only matters for very long videos. SnapDisk skips those files, lists them with the reason, and keeps going instead of failing the whole backup. NTFS has not been tested on a real disk yet, so we make no claim about it either way: not supported, not unsupported — untested.

Where do my photos go on the disk? By default SnapDisk copies from /sdcard/DCIM on your phone to /disk/DCIM on the external disk. Both folders can be changed in Settings — open the app and pick your own From and To folders. The app opened is a settings screen only; the backup itself is started from the notification.

Is SnapDisk on Google Play yet? Not yet — the Play listing is being prepared. Until then, install the v0.1.2 APK from the GitHub release page. It needs Android 7.0 or later.

Something does not work. Where do I report it? Open an issue on GitHub — every report gets an answer: github.com/dzianisv/photo-backup/issues. If a backup fails, the app shows the full error — copy it into the issue so the cause is visible, not guessed.
